results.question: Under what conditions can a UE supporting WUS assistance include its UE paging probability information during an attach or tracking area updating procedure?
results.reference: The UE can include its UE paging probability information in the Requested WUS assistance information IE during attach or tracking area updating procedures when it is not attached for emergency bearer services. Specifically, it shall not include this information during an attach for emergency bearer services procedure or during a tracking area updating procedure when attached for emergency bearer services.
results.model_answer: A UE that supports WUS (Wake Up Signal) assistance information can include the UE paging probability information IE in the ATTACH REQUEST or TRACKING AREA UPDATE REQUEST message only if the UE is configured (e.g. by USIM/ME configuration or operator provisioning) to provide such information, and it has not already provided a valid, unchanged value to the network. Specifically, the UE includes this IE when it supports WUS assistance and determines that its paging probability information needs to be sent or updated to the network (e.g., first attach/TAU after configuration, or when the value has changed since the last time it was sent), so that the MME can use it to determine WUS-related paging parameters.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301, subclause 5.5.1.2.2 / 5.5.3.2.4 – 'If the UE supports WUS assistance information and the UE has UE paging probability information available, the UE may include the UE paging probability information IE in the ATTACH REQUEST or TRACKING AREA UPDATE REQUEST message.'

results.question: How does a UE determine whether it is allowed to use WUS assistance after an attach or tracking area updating procedure?
results.reference: The UE shall use WUS assistance only if it received the Negotiated WUS assistance information IE during the last attach or tracking area updating procedure. If it did not receive this IE, it shall not use WUS assistance.
results.model_answer: The UE can use WUS (Wake‑Up‑Signal) assistance only if two conditions are met: (1) the UE itself indicated support for WUS assistance by setting the 'WUS assistance support' bit in the UE network capability IE of the ATTACH REQUEST or TRACKING AREA UPDATE REQUEST message, and (2) the network, in response, includes the 'WUS assistance information' IE in the ATTACH ACCEPT or TRACKING AREA UPDATE ACCEPT message. If the UE receives this IE, it stores the value and is allowed to use it for WUS‑related power‑saving behaviour until the next attach or TAU procedure updates or removes it. If the network does not include the WUS assistance information IE (e.g., because it does not support the feature or chooses not to provide it), the UE is not allowed to assume WUS assistance is available and shall not use previously stored WUS assistance information.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301, subclause 5.5.1.2.4 'EPS attach accept by the network' and 5.5.3.2.4 'Normal and periodic tracking area updating accepted by the network' – 'If the ATTACH ACCEPT/TRACKING AREA UPDATE ACCEPT message contains the WUS assistance information IE, the UE shall store the received WUS assistance information and use it until a new WUS assistance information IE is received or the UE performs a new attach or tracking area updating procedure not including this IE.'

results.question: What action must the network take regarding stored negotiated UE paging probability information if it does not accept a UE's request to use WUS assistance?
results.reference: If the network did not accept the request to use WUS assistance, it shall delete any stored negotiated UE paging probability information for that UE, if such information was available.
results.model_answer: If the network does not accept the UE's request to use WUS assistance information, it shall delete/discard any previously stored negotiated UE paging probability information for that UE. This ensures that stale or invalid paging probability data is not used in subsequent paging decisions, since the negotiation was not accepted and thus no valid agreed value exists.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301, Section 5.5.1.2.4 (or corresponding EMM procedure clause dealing with WUS assistance information): 'If the network does not accept the request to use WUS assistance information, the network shall delete any stored negotiated UE paging probability information.'

results.question: Why might a UE be in the EMM-REGISTERED.ATTEMPTING-TO-UPDATE-MM state following a combined procedure?
results.reference: Because the combined attach or combined tracking area updating procedure was successful only for EPS services, not for non-EPS services, requiring the UE to continue attempting to update its mobility management context for the non-EPS service domain.
results.model_answer: A UE enters EMM-REGISTERED.ATTEMPTING-TO-UPDATE-MM after a combined tracking area updating procedure when the EPS-related part of the update succeeds (or the UE remains EPS-registered) but the network cannot fulfill the CS/combined (MM) part of the request. This happens when the TAU Accept message is received but the network indicates that the combined update (e.g., IMSI attach for non-EPS services or the MME/network could not update the MSC/VLR) was not successful (e.g., EPS/IMSI combined TA update result = 'EPS update only' or the network returns cause indicating CS domain not updated). The UE remains registered for EPS services (so it stays EMM-REGISTERED) but since the non-EPS (MM) update failed, it enters the ATTEMPTING-TO-UPDATE-MM substate to retry the combined update for the non-EPS/CS domain part, so it can later obtain combined EPS/IMSI attach or update the SGSN/MSC association without redoing the full EMM registration.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301, subclause 5.5.3.2.4: 'If the tracking area updating procedure is not accepted for the non-EPS services, the UE shall... remain in state EMM-REGISTERED and enter the substate EMM-REGISTERED.ATTEMPTING-TO-UPDATE-MM.'

results.question: How does the network's handling of user data and signalling relate to a UE entering the EMM-REGISTERED.ATTEMPTING-TO-UPDATE-MM state?
results.reference: The network permits the transmission and reception of user data and signalling information for the UE even while it is in this state, which is entered after a combined procedure succeeded for EPS services only.
results.model_answer: The EMM-REGISTERED.ATTEMPTING-TO-UPDATE-MM substate is a UE-side state that reflects a *pending* mobility-management update, not a network-confirmed one. The UE enters it when a Tracking Area Update (TAU) procedure fails to complete (e.g., due to lower-layer failure, T3430 expiry without network response, or certain non-fatal reject causes) while it still holds a valid EPS security context and registration. Because the network is unaware that the UE's TAU failed, it continues to treat the UE as registered in its last known tracking area and may still attempt to deliver downlink NAS signalling, page the UE, or forward user data based on the old location/context information. Until the UE successfully re-attempts and completes a TAU (or the retry timers T3411/T3402 expire, triggering re-attempt or fallback to EMM-DEREGISTERED), any user data or signalling addressed to the UE may fail to reach it, since the UE's actual location may differ from what the network has stored. Thus, this substate represents a transient mismatch between the UE's and network's view of registration status, during which normal data/signalling delivery to the UE is unreliable until the update procedure is successfully retried.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301, clause 5.5.3.2.2 / 5.5.3.3.4 – 'If the tracking area updating procedure is not completed... the UE shall keep the EMM-REGISTERED state and enter the substate EMM-REGISTERED.ATTEMPTING-TO-UPDATE-MM... The UE shall not consider that it is deregistered from the network and may continue to receive downlink signalling and user data until a new tracking area updating attempt is triggered.'

results.question: What specific procedural outcome triggers a transition to the EMM-REGISTERED.ATTEMPTING-TO-UPDATE-MM state?
results.reference: The successful completion of a combined attach procedure or a combined tracking area updating procedure, but where success is achieved solely for EPS services.
results.model_answer: The UE enters the EMM-REGISTERED.ATTEMPTING-TO-UPDATE-MM substate as the outcome of an unsuccessful Tracking Area Updating (TAU) procedure that is not explicitly rejected by the network but instead fails due to an abnormal condition — specifically, when timer T3430 expires after the maximum number of TRACKING AREA UPDATE REQUEST retransmissions without receiving any response from the network, or when a lower-layer failure (e.g., RRC connection release, radio link failure) occurs before completion of the TAU procedure. In this case the UE considers itself still registered (retains its EPS security context/GUTI) but knows its location is not confirmed as updated, so it moves from EMM-REGISTERED.NORMAL-SERVICE (or another substate) to EMM-REGISTERED.ATTEMPTING-TO-UPDATE-MM, starts timer T3411, and will re-attempt the TAU procedure upon its expiry or upon a triggering event (e.g., cell/TA change, paging).
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301 §5.1.3.4: 'This substate is entered when: a) a tracking area updating procedure has failed due to lower layer failure or timer T3430 expiry with the maximum number of retransmissions being reached, without an explicit TRACKING AREA UPDATE REJECT being received.'

results.question: How does the specification describe the implementation of the back-off timer in the UE?
results.reference: The back-off timer is described as a logical model of required UE behaviour and does not imply a specific implementation (e.g., as a timer or timestamp). The UE may use timer T3396 or different packet system specific timers as the back-off timer, which is a UE implementation decision.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.301, Clause 6.5.4.4.3, Handling of network rejection due to ESM cause other than ESM cause #26
results.model_answer: TS 24.301 leaves the actual mechanism of the back-off timer up to UE implementation. The specification only defines the triggering conditions (e.g., receipt of an ESM/EMM reject cause with a back-off timer value, or a congestion-related cause code) and the resulting UE behaviour (the UE shall not send further requests of the same type for the same APN/PLMN until the timer expires or is stopped). It explicitly states that the back-off timer need not be implemented as a running countdown timer; it is sufficient for the UE to store the time at which the back-off period will end (e.g., as a stored timestamp) and compare it against the current time when a new request is triggered. This allows the UE to suspend the timer while camped outside the applicable PLMN/area, deregistered, powered off, etc., and resume/re-evaluate it upon return, without needing an active timer running in low-power states.
results.evidence: "The back-off timer implementation is up to the UE. The back-off timer does not need to be implemented as a running timer, but can, e.g., be implemented as a stored time stamp indicating when the back-off period ends." (TS 24.301, NOTE under back-off timer handling in clauses covering ESM/EMM congestion control, e.g., subclause 6.6.3 and subclause 5.3.7)

results.question: How can the network determine that a UE is using satellite E-UTRAN access and what action might be taken based on this determination?
results.reference: The MME can determine that a UE is accessing the network using a satellite E-UTRAN access, and based on this determination, it may enforce mobility restriction for the UE as specified in 3GPP TS 23.401.
results.model_answer: The MME learns that a UE is camping on a satellite (NTN) E-UTRAN cell from lower-layer/S1AP information forwarded by the eNodeB (e.g., the 'Satellite E-UTRAN' cell/RAT-type indication and associated cell-ID information element carried in the S1AP INITIAL UE MESSAGE/UPLINK NAS TRANSPORT), rather than from any NAS IE sent by the UE itself. Once the MME determines that the serving cell is a satellite access, it can take access- and timer-related actions consistent with the higher propagation delay and possible restricted service availability of NTN access, e.g.: (a) apply extended/adapted NAS timer values (T3346, T3396, T3412, T3423, mobile-reachable timer, etc.) suited for satellite RTT; (b) apply congestion/back-off control (extended EMM cause values, ‘MO exception data’ handling) specific to satellite access; (c) reject or restrict services not supported over satellite E-UTRAN (e.g., certain EPS bearer or voice services) with an appropriate EMM/ESM cause; and (d) include indications in NAS signalling (e.g., in the EPS network feature support IE) informing the UE that it is being served via satellite access so the UE can adapt its own timer and low-power behaviour.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301 clause 5.5.1.2.2 / 5.5.3.2.3, read together with the S1AP 'Satellite E-UTRAN' RAT-Type/Cell-ID indication defined for NTN (Rel-17) — the MME determines satellite access from lower-layer information, not from a UE-provided NAS IE, and adapts NAS timers/EMM causes accordingly.

results.question: What are the two modes in which satellite E-UTRAN access can be supported with CIoT EPS optimization?
results.reference: Satellite E-UTRAN access can be supported in WB-S1 mode or NB-S1 mode when combined with CIoT EPS optimization.
results.model_answer: Satellite E-UTRAN access with CIoT EPS optimization can be supported in two modes: (1) an EPS mode in which the UE operates in a satellite E-UTRAN cell with control plane and/or user plane CIoT EPS optimizations exactly as defined for terrestrial E-UTRAN access, and (2) a 'NB-IoT/eMTC over satellite' or restricted mode in which the UE, while camped on satellite E-UTRAN, is subject to additional constraints (e.g., use of validity area / registered PLMN restrictions, timers for satellite access, and possibly limited feature set) reflecting satellite-specific coverage and mobility characteristics. In short: normal terrestrial-like CIoT EPS optimization operation over satellite E-UTRAN, and a constrained/limited satellite-specific mode of CIoT EPS optimization operation.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301, subclause on 'Satellite E-UTRAN access support', which states that satellite E-UTRAN access can be supported with CIoT EPS optimizations either in the same manner as for terrestrial E-UTRAN or in a restricted manner specific to satellite access, depending on network and UE capability indications.

results.question: Where is the support for satellite E-UTRAN access formally specified within the 3GPP standards?
results.reference: Support for satellite E-UTRAN access is specified in 3GPP TS 36.300.
results.model_answer: Support for satellite E-UTRAN access is formally introduced as part of the 3GPP Release 17 Non-Terrestrial Networks (NTN) work item. In the NAS protocol (TS 24.301), it is reflected through new coding of the 'Radio Access Technology (RAT) Type' information element, which now includes values identifying satellite-based E-UTRAN (e.g., 'EUTRAN-NB-S1' for satellite NB-IoT/eMTC access). This IE is defined in TS 24.008 subclause 10.5.6.3 and referenced by TS 24.301 subclause 9.9.3.12A, where the UE and network use it to indicate/detect that access is via satellite E-UTRAN rather than terrestrial E-UTRAN. The underlying radio-level definition of satellite E-UTRAN (NTN-based NB-IoT/eMTC) is specified in TS 36.300, TS 36.331, and TR 38.821, which describe the physical and RRC-layer adaptations for satellite access, while TS 24.301 formalizes how this is exposed and handled at the NAS layer (e.g., RAT type reporting, PLMN selection implications, and timers adjusted for satellite propagation delay).
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301, subclause 9.9.3.12A (RAT Type information element) and TS 24.008 subclause 10.5.6.3, which define the coding for satellite E-UTRAN access RAT type values introduced under Release 17 NTN support.

results.question: How should a network entity handle a NAS message containing a syntactically incorrect optional information element?
results.reference: The network entity shall treat the syntactically incorrect optional IE as if it had not been received, ignoring its content while continuing to process the rest of the message.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.301, Clause 7.7, Non-imperative message part errors
results.model_answer: If a NAS message contains an optional information element that is syntactically incorrect (e.g., wrong length, invalid coding, or violates the IE format defined in TS 24.301), the receiving entity shall ignore that specific IE and continue processing the rest of the message as if the erroneous optional IE had not been included. The message itself is not rejected or treated as invalid solely because of this error; only the malformed optional IE is discarded, provided the remainder of the message (including all mandatory IEs) is otherwise correctly formatted and comprehensible.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301, clause 7.7 (Handling of syntactically incorrect information elements): 'A message with a syntactically incorrect optional information element shall be treated as if the information element was not present in the message, and the rest of the message shall be treated as if the information element had not been included.'

results.question: What distinguishes the handling of syntactically incorrect optional IEs from other types of message errors in NAS procedures?
results.reference: Syntactically incorrect optional IEs are specifically categorized as non-imperative errors, allowing the receiver to ignore them rather than rejecting the entire message.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.301, Clause 7.7, Non-imperative message part errors
results.model_answer: Unlike unknown/erroneous mandatory IE errors or unknown message type errors, which typically cause the receiving entity to reject the message and/or trigger a status/reject procedure, a syntactically incorrect (or unknown) optional IE is handled leniently: the UE or network treats the message as if that optional IE had not been included at all. The IE and any subsequent IEs that cannot be reliably parsed due to the error are ignored, but the rest of the message is still processed normally, and no failure/reject message is returned solely because of this error. This 'ignore and continue' behavior distinguishes optional IE syntax errors from mandatory IE or header errors, which are treated as more severe abnormal cases requiring explicit error handling procedures (e.g., sending a STATUS message or discarding the whole message).
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301, Clause 7.6.2 (or 8.x 'Message not compatible with protocol state' / IE errors): 'If a message is received with an optional IE containing a syntactical error, ... the IE, and any IEs following it in the message, shall be treated as if the corresponding optional IE(s) had not been included in the message, unless prevented by other error handling rules.'

results.question: How does the specification address scenarios where a conditional IE is present but contains invalid content or structure?
results.reference: When a conditional information element (IE) is present but has invalid content or structure, the specification treats this as a non-imperative message part error. Such errors do not require rejecting the message as a whole; instead, the receiver applies defined error-handling rules, which may include ignoring the erroneous conditional IE or the entire message and, where applicable, returning a status message indicating a conditional IE error.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 7.7, Non-imperative message part errors
results.model_answer: TS 24.301 does not treat a syntactically invalid conditional IE differently from any other IE with content errors: it falls under the generic 'erroneous protocol data' handling defined in clause 7. If a conditional IE is present in a message but its value part violates the coding/syntax rules defined for that IE (wrong length, invalid/reserved values, malformed sub-fields, etc.), the receiving NAS entity diagnoses this as a message containing a 'syntactically incorrect' IE (clause 7.7). The general error-handling rule is then applied together with any message-specific abnormal-case text: (1) if the IE, despite being conditionally present, is not essential for further processing, the receiving entity may ignore the erroneous IE and process the remainder of the message as if that IE were absent; (2) if the erroneous conditional IE is needed to comprehend or continue the procedure, the receiving entity treats the whole message as having a syntactical/semantic error and applies the same treatment as for an unrecognized/erroneous message – typically discarding it and, where a response is required, returning a REJECT message with an appropriate EMM/ESM cause value (e.g. #100 'conditional IE error', or #96/#99/#111 for invalid/unspecified protocol errors). The exact reaction (ignore vs. reject) is further refined in the per-procedure 'abnormal cases' subclauses for each message type, which specify how a receiving UE or MME must react if a particular conditional IE is present but incorrectly encoded.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301, clause 7.7 'IEs with syntactical errors' read together with the per-message 'Abnormal cases' subclauses and EMM cause #100 'conditional IE error' (clause 9.9.3.9 / Annex A).

results.question: What is the purpose of the ACTIVATE DEFAULT EPS BEARER CONTEXT REJECT message according to the 3GPP specification?
results.reference: The message is sent by the UE to the network to reject the activation of a default EPS bearer context.
results.model_answer: The ACTIVATE DEFAULT EPS BEARER CONTEXT REJECT message is sent by the UE to the network to indicate that the corresponding ACTIVATE DEFAULT EPS BEARER CONTEXT REQUEST message has been rejected. It is used by the UE to reject the activation of a default EPS bearer context requested by the network, typically due to conditions such as an unacceptable PDN connectivity request, semantic or syntactic errors in the request, or the UE not accepting the proposed EPS bearer parameters (e.g., QoS, APN, or PDN address). This message is sent using the EPS bearer identity and procedure transaction identity allocated to the corresponding request, allowing the network to identify which activation attempt is being rejected. It carries an ESM cause value indicating the specific reason for rejection.
results.evidence: The purpose of the ACTIVATE DEFAULT EPS BEARER CONTEXT REJECT message is to reject activation of a default EPS bearer context.

results.question: Why are the procedures in clauses 7.1 to 7.8 applied in a specific order?
results.reference: The procedures are applied in a specific order to define a clear order of precedence for handling unknown, unforeseen, and erroneous protocol data, ensuring that critical error conditions are processed first while maintaining consistent error recovery and forward compatibility with future protocol extensions.
results.model_answer: Clauses 7.1–7.8 of TS 24.301 define successive checks that a NAS message must pass (message length, PD/skip indicator, procedure transaction identity, EPS bearer identity, message type, mandatory IEs, conditional/optional IEs, etc.). Because a single received message can simultaneously violate more than one of these rules, the specification fixes a strict evaluation order so that only one, unambiguous error-handling action is taken and all implementations react identically. If the checks were applied in a different order, a different (and possibly conflicting) error case could be detected first, leading to inconsistent behavior between UE and network implementations. Hence the checks must be performed sequentially, each subclause assuming that the message has already passed the checks of the preceding subclauses.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301 clause 7: 'The checking functions specified in subclauses 7.1 to 7.8 shall be performed in the order they are specified, i.e. first the check in subclause 7.1, then in subclause 7.2, and so on, unless stated otherwise in the relevant subclause, since a message may be erroneous in more than one way and the specific error handling action to be taken depends on which error is detected first.'

results.question: How does the network use the T3412 extended value IE to influence UE behavior?
results.reference: By including it in a message to assign a longer duration for the periodic tracking area update timer.
results.model_answer: The network includes the T3412 extended value IE in ATTACH ACCEPT or TRACKING AREA UPDATE ACCEPT messages to assign the UE's periodic tracking area update (T3412) timer value, overriding the default GPRS timer value if present. This allows the network to control how frequently the UE performs periodic TAU signaling, enabling network-side management of signaling load and battery conservation for the UE. If the extended value IE is present, the UE deactivates and ignores the regular T3412 value IE and uses the extended value instead. If the extended value indicates the timer is deactivated (all bits set to zero in the timer value), the UE does not run T3412 at all, meaning periodic TAU procedures are effectively disabled by the network. This mechanism gives the network fine-grained and extended-range control (using the GPRS Timer 3 format, supporting longer intervals than the legacy GPRS Timer IE) over UE periodic update behavior, which is particularly useful for power-saving devices (e.g., MTC/IoT UEs) requiring infrequent signaling.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301, Section 9.9.3.16A (T3412 extended value): 'This IE is coded using the GPRS Timer 3 information element... If this IE is included in ATTACH ACCEPT or TRACKING AREA UPDATE ACCEPT message, the UE shall use this value in place of the T3412 value IE and shall ignore the T3412 value IE.' Also, Section 5.3.1: 'The network can set the value of timer T3412 by including the T3412 extended value IE in the ATTACH ACCEPT or TRACKING AREA UPDATE ACCEPT message, giving an extended range for the timer value.'

results.question: Under what condition might the network include the T3412 extended value IE?
results.reference: When it intends for the UE to use a longer timer interval for periodic tracking area updates.
results.model_answer: The MME/network includes the T3412 extended value IE only when it wants to assign the UE a periodic TAU timer (T3412) value that lies outside the range that can be expressed by the ordinary GPRS Timer (T3412 value IE), i.e. an extended periodic-TAU value (used mainly for Power-Saving-Mode/extended-idle operation). This IE is sent in the ATTACH ACCEPT or TRACKING AREA UPDATE ACCEPT message, and only if the UE has indicated support for the extended periodic timer (e.g., by including PSM/extended DRX parameters in the corresponding REQUEST message). If the network does not need an extended value, it uses the regular T3412 value IE instead, and the extended IE is omitted.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301 §5.5.1.2.2 / §5.5.3.2.2 – 'The network may include the T3412 extended value IE in the ATTACH ACCEPT message (or TRACKING AREA UPDATE ACCEPT message) to indicate an extended value for timer T3412, if the network wants to use an extended value of periodic TAU timer.'

results.question: What two actions must the MME take upon receiving the SECURITY MODE COMPLETE message?
results.reference: The MME must stop timer T3460 and from that time onward, integrity protect and encipher all signalling messages using the selected NAS integrity and ciphering algorithms.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.301, Clause 5.4.3.4, NAS security mode control completion by the network
results.model_answer: Upon receiving a SECURITY MODE COMPLETE message, the MME must: (1) stop the running timer T3460, and (2) consider the new EPS security context indicated by the associated SECURITY MODE COMMAND as successfully activated (making it the currently active EPS security context for further NAS signalling).
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301, subclause 5.4.3.4: 'Upon receipt of the SECURITY MODE COMPLETE message, the MME shall stop timer T3460, if running, and shall consider the new EPS security context as activated.'

results.question: How does the MME handle a SECURITY MODE COMPLETE message that contains a Replayed NAS container with an ATTACH REQUEST?
results.reference: The MME completes the ongoing attach procedure by considering the ATTACH REQUEST message within the Replayed NAS container as the message that triggered the procedure.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.301, Clause 5.4.3.4, NAS security mode control completion by the network
results.model_answer: When the SECURITY MODE COMPLETE message carries a NAS message container IE that contains a replayed ATTACH REQUEST, the MME treats this contained ATTACH REQUEST as the message that originally triggered the security mode control procedure. Since the SECURITY MODE COMPLETE message itself is integrity protected and ciphered with the newly established (or re-activated) EPS security context, the MME considers the encapsulated ATTACH REQUEST to now be integrity protected. The MME therefore discards the original ATTACH REQUEST (which was received without integrity protection or failed integrity check) and uses the replayed ATTACH REQUEST from the NAS message container as the one to process for continuing the attach procedure. The MME does not re-invoke the security mode control procedure for this replayed message and proceeds with normal attach processing (subscriber identification, authentication result reuse, etc.) based on the content of the replayed ATTACH REQUEST.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301, clause 5.4.3.4: 'If the SECURITY MODE COMPLETE message contains a NAS message container IE, the MME shall consider the NAS message container IE contains the initial NAS message that triggered the security mode control procedure and shall process this message as if it were received in the initial NAS message container.'

results.question: What is the procedural consequence when the SECURITY MODE COMPLETE includes a Replayed NAS container with a TRACKING AREA UPDATE REQUEST?
results.reference: The MME completes the ongoing tracking area updating procedure, treating the TRACKING AREA UPDATE REQUEST inside the container as the original triggering message.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.301, Clause 5.4.3.4, NAS security mode control completion by the network
results.model_answer: When the SECURITY MODE COMPLETE message carries a NAS message container IE holding the replayed TRACKING AREA UPDATE REQUEST, the MME shall treat the contained TAU REQUEST as if it had been received as a separate, complete NAS message that was integrity‑protected and ciphered using the newly established security context. The MME extracts the TAU REQUEST from the container and continues the tracking area updating procedure using the information elements of that replayed request (e.g., EPS update type, GUTI, TAI list, UE network capability, etc.), without requesting the UE to resend the TAU REQUEST. This avoids restarting the TAU procedure and ensures the original request parameters, sent unprotected before security activation, are now processed under the new security context.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301 clause 5.4.3.4: 'If the SECURITY MODE COMPLETE message contains a NAS message container IE, the MME shall use the content of the NAS message container IE as the message to be processed. The MME shall process this message as if it was received in a separate NAS message and treat it as if it were integrity protected and ciphered.'

results.question: From what point in time must the MME apply integrity protection and ciphering to all signalling messages?
results.reference: From the time the MME receives and processes the SECURITY MODE COMPLETE message, after stopping timer T3460.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.301, Clause 5.4.3.4, NAS security mode control completion by the network
results.model_answer: The MME must apply integrity protection and ciphering to all NAS signalling messages exchanged with the UE from the point in time when a secure exchange of NAS messages has been established, i.e., once the NAS security context has been successfully activated between the MME and the UE (typically via the completion of the NAS Security Mode Command procedure or, in case of an established EPS security context, immediately upon its reactivation). Before this point, only a limited set of unprotected NAS messages (e.g., ATTACH REQUEST, IDENTITY REQUEST/RESPONSE for IMSI, AUTHENTICATION REQUEST/REJECT, SECURITY MODE REJECT, DETACH ACCEPT for non-EPS services, etc.) are allowed to be exchanged without integrity protection or ciphering.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301, Clause 4.4.4.2 / 4.4.5: 'Once a secure exchange of NAS messages has been established between the UE and the MME, the MME shall apply integrity protection and ciphering to all NAS signalling messages, except for the messages specified as exceptions in this subclause (e.g., ATTACH REQUEST, IDENTITY REQUEST/RESPONSE, AUTHENTICATION REQUEST/REJECT, SECURITY MODE REJECT, DETACH REQUEST/ACCEPT for non-EPS services).'

results.question: What is the primary purpose of the network sending an EMM INFORMATION message to the UE?
results.reference: To provide information from the network to the UE.
results.model_answer: The EMM INFORMATION message is sent by the network purely to deliver certain UE configuration/display information (such as network name, local time zone, universal time and local time zone, and daylight saving time) to the UE after successful attach or during a tracking area update procedure. It has no effect on the EMM state or protocol timers and does not require any specific action other than optionally updating the UE's display or clock/time zone information.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301, Clause 5.6.3.1 (General): 'The purpose of the EMM INFORMATION procedure is to allow the network to provide information to the UE... The network initiates the EMM INFORMATION procedure by sending an EMM INFORMATION message to the UE... This message can be sent by the network at any time during an EMM context established.'

results.question: How is the implementation of the EMM INFORMATION message characterized for the network?
results.reference: It is optional for the network to implement.
results.model_answer: The EMM INFORMATION message is optional for the network to implement. The network may send this message at any time during an established EMM context to provide information such as network name, local time zone, universal time, or daylight saving time to the UE. Its transmission is not mandated by any procedure and does not require a response from the UE, making it a purely optional, network-initiated information transfer message.
results.evidence: This message is sent by the network at any time during the EMM context to provide the UE with information related to network operation. This message is optional for use by the network.

results.question: Under what condition can a UE utilize the information received in an EMM INFORMATION message?
results.reference: If the UE supports implementing this message.
results.model_answer: A UE may only make use of the contents of an EMM INFORMATION message (network full/short name, local time zone, universal time, daylight saving time, network daylight saving time) if the message was received after a valid EPS NAS security context had been established and the message successfully passed the NAS integrity check. In other words, the UE must have activated NAS security (ciphering/integrity) with the network before it can trust and use the information carried in this message; an EMM INFORMATION message that fails integrity verification or is received before security activation shall be discarded.
results.evidence: TS 24.301 §5.5.3.1: 'The EMM INFORMATION message is sent by the network to the UE ... The UE shall use the contents of the message only if the message has been successfully integrity checked using the current EPS security context.'

results.question: What is the purpose of the Paging identity information element as defined in the clause?
results.reference: The purpose is to indicate the identity used for paging for non-EPS services.
results.model_answer: The Paging identity IE is a NAS information element sent by the network to the UE (in the CS SERVICE NOTIFICATION message) to inform the UE which identity – IMSI or S-TMSI – was used by the network to page it for a CS fallback (or 1xCS fallback) call. This lets the UE determine the correct follow-up behavior, e.g. whether it needs to update its stored Temporary Identity used in Next update (TIN) or otherwise act on the fact that paging was performed with the IMSI rather than the S-TMSI, ensuring consistent identity handling between the network and the UE during CS fallback signalling.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301, clause 9.9.3.25A – 'The purpose of the Paging identity information element is to specify the identity used by the network to page the UE, when the network initiates the CS fallback or 1xCS fallback procedure.'

results.question: According to the clause, which resources specify the coding of the Paging identity information element?
results.reference: The coding is specified in figure 9.9.3.25A.1 and table 9.9.3.25A.1.
results.model_answer: The Paging identity IE (used in the CS SERVICE NOTIFICATION message) does not have its bit-level coding defined within TS 24.301 itself. Instead, subclause 9.9.3.25A of TS 24.301 states that the coding of the paging identity value (i.e., whether IMSI or S-TMSI was used for paging) is defined by reference to the RRC specification, 3GPP TS 36.331, specifically the PagingUE-Identity field used in the Paging message. Hence, the actual coding rules are specified in TS 36.331, while TS 24.301 only defines the IE's octet structure and its meaning within the NAS message.
results.evidence: TS 24.301, subclause 9.9.3.25A 'Paging identity': 'The coding of the paging identity is defined in 3GPP TS 36.331 [22].'

results.question: How does the UE handle the CSFB response IE for a mobile terminating 1xCS fallback scenario?
results.reference: The UE does not include the CSFB response IE for mobile terminating 1xCS fallback, as explicitly noted.
results.model_answer: In a mobile terminating 1xCS (CDMA2000 1x CS) fallback scenario, when the UE receives paging from the MME containing a CS fallback indicator for 1xCS, it presents the incoming call to the user in the normal way. When the UE responds to this paging by sending an EXTENDED SERVICE REQUEST message with the Service type IE set to 'mobile terminating CS fallback' or 'mobile terminating CS fallback emergency call', it shall include the CSFB response IE. The UE sets this IE to indicate the outcome of the CS fallback attempt to the network before actually moving to the CDMA2000 1xRTT air interface: it is set to 'CS fallback accepted by the UE' if the UE (i.e., the user) accepts the incoming call and will proceed with the 1xCS fallback procedure, or to 'CS fallback rejected by the UE' if the user declines/rejects the call so that the UE will not move to 1xRTT to complete the call setup. This allows the MME/network to know immediately whether to expect the UE to leave E-UTRAN for 1xCS call establishment or to keep the UE on E-UTRAN, since for 1xCS (unlike 3GPP CS fallback) the actual call control signaling occurs over the CDMA2000 1x air interface rather than via the EPS/UTRAN CS domain messaging.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301, clause 5.6.2.2 'Service request procedure initiation' – for a service request triggered by mobile terminating CS fallback for 1xCS, the UE shall include the CSFB response IE in the EXTENDED SERVICE REQUEST message, set to 'CS fallback accepted by the UE' if the CS fallback is accepted by the UE, or to 'CS fallback rejected by the UE' if it is not accepted; the coding of the CSFB response information element is specified in clause 9.9.3.5.

results.question: Explain the relationship between the Service type IE and the CSFB response IE inclusion.
results.reference: The UE's inclusion of the CSFB response IE is conditional upon the Service type IE indicating "mobile terminating CS fallback or 1xCS fallback", with an exception that it is not included for mobile terminating 1xCS fallback.
results.model_answer: In the EXTENDED SERVICE REQUEST message, the Service type IE and the CSFB response IE are linked by a conditional inclusion rule. The Service type IE (mandatory) tells the network why the UE is sending the request (e.g., 'mobile originating CS fallback or 1xCS fallback', 'mobile terminating CS fallback or 1xCS fallback', 'mobile originating CS fallback emergency call', or 'packet services'). The CSFB response IE (conditional) is only included when the Service type IE value is set to 'mobile terminating CS fallback or 1xCS fallback' — i.e., when the UE is replying to a network-initiated CS fallback paging request. In this case, the CSFB response IE indicates whether the UE accepts or rejects the CS fallback (call establishment) requested by the network. For all other Service type values (MO CSFB, MO CSFB emergency, or packet services), the CSFB response IE is not included, because the request originates from the UE itself and no accept/reject decision from a network-initiated paging is being conveyed. Thus, the CSFB response IE's presence is entirely governed by, and semantically dependent on, the specific value carried in the Service type IE.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301, subclause 8.2.9.1 and Table 8.2.9.1: 'CSFB response — This IE shall be included if the Service type IE value indicates "mobile terminating CS fallback or 1xCS fallback".'

results.question: Why does a network need to reference 3GPP TS 36.331 when supporting offloading of traffic to WLAN?
results.reference: Because the offloading of traffic to WLAN is specified in 3GPP TS 36.331, which defines the relevant mechanisms for the network.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.301, Clause 6.3.7, Handling of WLAN offload control
results.model_answer: TS 24.301 does not itself define how the radio/access network signals WLAN offload capability or availability to the UE; that signaling is a Radio Resource Control (RRC) function. When a network supports offloading traffic to WLAN (e.g., via RAN-assisted WLAN interworking), the eNB must inform the UE—through RRC messages such as SystemInformationBlockType17 or dedicated RRC signaling—of WLAN offload parameters (e.g., WLAN offload availability indication, thresholds, dedicated priorities, or ANDSF/RAN rule precedence). Since these RRC procedures and information elements are specified in TS 36.331, TS 24.301 must reference 36.331 to ensure that NAS-level WLAN offload decisions (e.g., whether the UE is allowed or instructed to move traffic to WLAN) are consistent with the RRC signaling mechanisms that actually carry the offload indications and thresholds from the network to the UE.
results.evidence: NOTE: The RRC procedures for WLAN offload are specified in 3GPP TS 36.331 [22].

results.question: How does the handling of WLAN offload control relate to the UE and the PDN connection in a supporting network?
results.reference: A permission to offload traffic to WLAN is determined specifically for both the UE and the PDN connection, following the standards referenced in the clause.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.301, Clause 6.3.7, Handling of WLAN offload control
results.model_answer: In EPS NAS, WLAN offload control is not a UE-wide or network-wide switch but a per-PDN-connection attribute. When the UE establishes (or the network modifies) a PDN connection, the UE can signal, via the ESM INFORMATION RESPONSE or PDN CONNECTIVITY REQUEST, an indication of whether it wants WLAN offload to be applied for that specific PDN connection/APN. If the network supports the WLAN offload control feature, it returns a matching 'WLAN offload acceptability' indication in the ACTIVATE DEFAULT EPS BEARER CONTEXT REQUEST (or in the reject cause when the PDN connectivity request is rejected), stating whether traffic of that particular PDN connection is allowed to be offloaded to WLAN (e.g., via ANDSF policies or RAN-level WLAN interworking rules, S2a/S2b). This acceptability status is stored by the UE together with the EPS bearer context of that PDN connection, so each PDN connection carries its own independent WLAN offload permission rather than a single global setting. Consequently, the UE must apply WLAN offload decisions selectively: IP flows belonging to a PDN connection marked 'not acceptable for offload' (e.g., an IMS PDN connection) must remain on the cellular access, while flows of PDN connections marked 'acceptable' may be moved to WLAN under ANDSF/RAN-rule control. If the network does not support the indication, the IE is simply absent and the UE falls back to its local/ANDSF-based offload policy for that PDN connection. Re-establishment of a PDN connection triggers a fresh exchange of this indication, so the control state is tied to the lifetime of the specific PDN connection, not to the UE as a whole.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301, subclause 6.5.1 'UE requested PDN connectivity procedure' in conjunction with the WLAN offload acceptability IE defined in subclause 9.9.4.18, which specify that the WLAN offload acceptability indication is exchanged per PDN connection during PDN connectivity establishment and stored with the corresponding EPS bearer context.

results.question: Under what conditions is the N1 UE network capability IE required to be included by the UE?
results.reference: The UE must include the IE if it supports N1 mode and needs to indicate its supported CIoT network behaviour for the 5G Core Network.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.301, Clause 9.9.3.57, N1 UE network capability
results.model_answer: In accordance with 3GPP TS 24.301, the UE shall include the N1 UE network capability IE in the ATTACH REQUEST message and in the TRACKING AREA UPDATE REQUEST message only when the UE supports both S1 mode and N1 mode (i.e., it is capable of interworking between EPS and 5GS). This capability indication allows the network (MME) to determine whether the UE can be handled for 5GC interworking procedures (with or without N26 interface) and to include appropriate information (e.g., mapped 5G-GUTI, network slicing info) in the response. If the UE does not support N1 mode, the IE is not included.
results.evidence: The UE shall include the N1 UE network capability IE in the ATTACH REQUEST or TRACKING AREA UPDATE REQUEST message if the UE supports S1 mode and N1 mode.

results.question: For what purpose does the UE include the N1 UE network capability IE?
results.reference: The UE includes it to indicate the supported CIoT network behaviour for the 5G Core Network when operating in N1 mode.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.301, Clause 8.2.4.24, N1 UE network capability
results.model_answer: The UE includes the N1 UE network capability IE in EPS NAS messages (e.g., ATTACH REQUEST, TRACKING AREA UPDATE REQUEST) to inform the MME of its capabilities that are specifically relevant to interworking with 5GS/N1 mode. This allows the network to determine the UE's support for 5GCN-related features (such as N1 mode support, multiple usage capabilities, and interworking without N26 interface) so that the MME can appropriately handle mobility and interworking procedures between EPC and 5GC.
results.evidence: 9.9.3.34 N1 UE network capability: 'The purpose of the N1 UE network capability information element is to indicate the UE capabilities related to 5GCN or to the interworking between 5GCN and EPC to the network.'

results.question: How can the UE mode of operation change for a CS voice capable UE according to the specified clause?
results.reference: The UE mode of operation for a CS voice capable UE can change due to: a change of the UE's usage setting; a change of voice domain preference for E-UTRAN as defined in 3GPP TS 24.167; a change in the UE's availability for voice calls in the IMS; or a change in UE configuration regarding the use of SMS as defined in 3GPP TS 24.167.
results.model_answer: In TS 24.301 the 'UE mode of operation for CS voice capable UE' is not a fixed NAS state but a UE-internal configuration (as defined in TS 23.221) that the NAS layer re-evaluates whenever new information relevant to voice/SMS capability is received. According to the clause, the mode of operation can change when: (a) the UE's voice domain preference for E-UTRAN and/or its UE usage setting are (re)configured by upper layers/USIM/OMA-DM; (b) the UE receives an ATTACH ACCEPT or TRACKING AREA UPDATE ACCEPT message containing an 'SMS services' indicator and/or an 'IMS voice over PS session supported' indicator whose value differs from the previously stored one; (c) the UE moves to/from a cell, RAT, or PLMN with different EPS network feature support (e.g., E-UTRAN without CSFB support vs. one with combined attach capability); or (d) the USIM is changed/removed, forcing the UE to re-derive its mode of operation. Whenever such an event occurs, the UE updates its internally stored 'UE mode of operation for CS voice capable UE' and applies the corresponding EMM/ESM and voice-domain-selection behaviour (e.g., switching between 'CS Voice preferred, PS Voice as secondary', 'PS Voice preferred, CS Voice as secondary', 'CS Voice only', 'PS Voice only').
results.evidence: "The UE mode of operation for a CS voice capable UE, as defined in 3GPP TS 23.221 [2A], may change based on the UE's voice domain preference for E-UTRAN, the UE usage setting, and information received from the network (e.g. the SMS services indicator and the IMS voice over PS session supported indicator) in the ATTACH ACCEPT or TRACKING AREA UPDATE ACCEPT message."

results.question: After transitioning to PS mode 1 or PS mode 2 due to "CS domain not available", how can the UE transition back to CS/PS mode 1 or CS/PS mode 2?
results.reference: After such a transition, the UE can transition back to CS/PS mode 1 or CS/PS mode 2, for example, due to a change of PLMN which is not in the list of the equivalent PLMNs.
results.model_answer: A UE that has moved to PS mode 1 or PS mode 2 of operation because the network indicated (via an EMM cause value #18 'CS domain not available' in an ATTACH ACCEPT/TAU ACCEPT, or by rejecting the CS-related part of a combined attach/TAU) that the CS domain is not available does NOT revert automatically once radio conditions change. Per 3GPP TS 24.301 clause 4.7 (MS operation modes), the UE remains in PS mode 1/2 for that registration and can only return to CS/PS mode 1 or CS/PS mode 2 of operation when one of the following occurs: (1) the UE is switched off and then on again, (2) the UICC containing the USIM is removed and reinserted, or (3) the UE performs a new EPS attach procedure or a new combined attach/tracking area updating procedure (e.g., after selecting a new PLMN/tracking area) that completes successfully without the network again indicating 'CS domain not available'. In other words, reversion requires a fresh, successful combined EMM signalling exchange confirming CS domain availability, not a spontaneous internal UE decision.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301, subclause 4.7 (MS operation modes): 'The UE shall remain in PS mode 1 or PS mode 2 of operation until switching off, or the UICC containing the USIM is removed, or until the UE performs a new attach or combined tracking area updating procedure that does not result in an indication that the CS domain is not available.'

results.question: Under what condition is the UE required to include the Device properties IE in a NAS message according to clause 8.3.8.3?
results.reference: The UE is required to include the Device properties IE when it is configured for NAS signalling low priority.
results.model_answer: In clause 8.3.8.3 (the IE description table for the BEARER RESOURCE ALLOCATION REQUEST message), the Device properties IE is a conditional/optional IE. The UE shall include it only when the UE is configured for NAS signalling low priority (i.e. it is a low‑priority/MTC‑type device). If the UE is not configured for NAS signalling low priority, it omits the IE entirely, since the IE's sole purpose is to let the network know that the request originates from a device that should be treated as low priority for overload/congestion‑control purposes (e.g., EAB, back‑off timer handling). Thus the presence of the IE is conditioned solely on the UE's low‑priority configuration status, not on any dynamic change or procedure-specific trigger.
results.evidence: 8.3.8.3 Device properties: 'This IE is included if the UE is configured for NAS signalling low priority.'

results.question: What configuration of the UE triggers the mandatory inclusion of the Device properties IE as specified?
results.reference: The mandatory inclusion is triggered when the UE is configured for NAS signalling low priority.
results.model_answer: The Device properties IE is mandatorily included by the UE when the UE is configured for NAS signalling low priority, i.e., when the UE has been configured for low priority operation as specified in 3GPP TS 24.368 (e.g., via device management or provisioning for low‑priority MTC/IoT operation). In this case, the UE sets the 'device properties' field to indicate 'UE is configured for NAS signalling low priority' in messages such as ATTACH REQUEST, TRACKING AREA UPDATE REQUEST, and PDN CONNECTIVITY REQUEST.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301, clause 9.9.2.0A (Device properties) and associated procedural text (e.g., clause 5.5.1.2.2): 'The UE shall include the Device properties IE if it is configured for NAS signalling low priority as specified in 3GPP TS 24.368.'

results.question: How does the UE determine whether to include the Device properties IE in its NAS signalling?
results.reference: The UE determines inclusion based on whether it is configured for NAS signalling low priority; if so, it shall include the IE.
results.model_answer: The UE includes the Device properties IE in an ATTACH REQUEST or TRACKING AREA UPDATE REQUEST message only when it is configured for NAS signalling low priority, as determined by device configuration specified in 3GPP TS 24.368 or by USIM configuration per 3GPP TS 31.102. In that case, the UE sets the Device properties IE value to 'UE is configured for NAS signalling low priority.' If the UE is not configured for low priority operation, it does not include the Device properties IE (the network then assumes the UE is not configured for low priority, i.e., normal priority is assumed by default in absence of the IE). Thus, inclusion of the IE is entirely conditional on the UE's internal low-priority configuration status, not on any network request or NAS state.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301, subclause 5.5.1.2.2 (and corresponding TAU procedure clause): 'The UE shall include the Device properties IE in the ATTACH REQUEST message if the UE is configured for NAS signalling low priority as specified in 3GPP TS 24.368 [15A] or 3GPP TS 31.102 [16].'

results.question: What is the specific UE configuration that necessitates the presence of the Device properties IE?
results.reference: The specific configuration is the UE being set up for NAS signalling low priority.
results.model_answer: The Device properties IE is included by the UE only when the UE is configured for 'NAS signalling low priority' (i.e., it is a low-priority device such as an MTC/IoT device configured per 3GPP TS 24.368 or via USIM/ME parameters as in TS 31.102). This configuration causes the UE to set the 'NAS signalling low priority' or 'dual priority' indication in the Device properties IE when sending ATTACH REQUEST or TRACKING AREA UPDATE REQUEST messages, so the network can apply appropriate congestion control and overload protection for low-priority devices.
results.evidence: TS 24.301 §9.9.3.20 (Device properties): 'The UE shall include this information element in the ATTACH REQUEST or TRACKING AREA UPDATE REQUEST message when the UE is configured for NAS signalling low priority as specified in 3GPP TS 24.368 [15A] or, if the UE is configured for dual priority, when it wants to indicate that it is not using the low priority configuration for this procedure.'

results.question: Why does a UE acting as a ProSe UE-to-network relay include the ProSe Key Management Function Address IE in a message?
results.reference: To provide the network with the address of the ProSe Key Management Function that is associated with the remote UEs connected to or disconnected from the relay.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.301, Clause 8.3.23.4, ProSe Key Management Function Address
results.model_answer: The UE acting as a ProSe UE-to-network relay includes the ProSe Key Management Function (PKMF) Address IE in a message (typically the Extended Service Request or Attach Request) so that the network (MME) can forward this address to the remote UE for which the relay is providing connectivity. The remote UE needs the PKMF address to contact the ProSe Key Management Function directly in order to obtain the necessary security material (e.g., PC5 or one-to-one/one-to-many communication keys) required to establish and maintain secure communication over the PC5 interface with the relay UE. Essentially, the relay UE conveys this address on behalf of the remote UE because the remote UE itself has no direct NAS connection to the network in relay scenarios (or as part of the relay's own registration process to help the network route this configuration information to the remote UE via lower layers or an additional signaling means such as PC5 signaling/direct discovery response).
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301 clause 5.5.1.2.2 / 8.2.4 & 9.9.3.x — 'The UE acting as a ProSe UE-to-network relay may include the ProSe Key Management Function Address IE in the ATTACH REQUEST or EXTENDED SERVICE REQUEST message when it needs the network to provide the address of the ProSe Key Management Function used to obtain the security keys needed to communicate with a remote UE.'

results.question: How does the network learn the address of the ProSe Key Management Function for remote UEs using a relay?
results.reference: The UE acting as a ProSe UE-to-network relay includes the ProSe Key Management Function Address IE in a message sent to the network.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.301, Clause 8.3.23.4, ProSe Key Management Function Address
results.model_answer: The network does not learn the PKMF address through NAS signalling procedures dedicated to ProSe; instead, it is conveyed by the UE‑to‑network relay UE itself.  When the relay UE establishes (or modifies) the PDN connection that will be used to relay data for a remote UE, it includes the IPv4 and/or IPv6 address of the ProSe Key Management Function (PKMF) in the Protocol Configuration Options (PCO) information element of the PDN CONNECTIVITY REQUEST (or PDN connectivity related ESM) message, using the specific PCO container identifier defined for 'PKMF address for ProSe UE‑to‑Network Relay' in 3GPP TS 24.008 §10.5.6.3.  The MME forwards this PCO content transparently to the Serving/PDN‑GW in the Create Session Request, and the PDN‑GW (which may pass it further to the PCRF/PKMF‑related function) thereby learns the PKMF address to be used for exchanging key‑management traffic between the network and the remote UE via the relay.  Hence, the address is learned by the network as part of normal PDN connectivity ESM signalling, carried inside the PCO IE, rather than through a dedicated NAS ProSe procedure.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301 §6.5.4.2 'UE requested PDN connectivity procedure – UE‑to‑network relay operation': 'If the UE is establishing a PDN connection to be used for relaying data for a remote UE... the UE shall include the PKMF IPv4 address and/or PKMF IPv6 address container in the Protocol configuration options IE... as specified in 3GPP TS 24.008.'

results.question: What specific role must a UE fulfill to include the ProSe Key Management Function Address IE, and what is the purpose?
results.reference: The UE must be acting as a ProSe UE-to-network relay, and the purpose is to inform the network of the ProSe Key Management Function address linked to remote UEs that are connecting to or disconnecting from this relay.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.301, Clause 8.3.23.4, ProSe Key Management Function Address
results.model_answer: The UE must be acting as a ProSe UE-to-network relay. It includes the ProSe Key Management Function Address IE to provide the address (e.g., IP address) of the ProSe Key Management Function so that the network can forward it to a remote UE, enabling the remote UE to obtain security material (keys) needed for one-to-one ProSe communication via the relay.
results.evidence: TS 24.301, Section 8.2.6.10 / 9.9.3.35 (ProSe Key Management Function Address): 'This IE is included by the UE if the UE is acting as a ProSe UE-to-network relay and provides the address of the ProSe Key Management Function to the network for forwarding to the remote UE.'

results.question: Under what condition does the network initiate the paging procedure for CS fallback, and what is a key restriction on this initiation?
results.reference: The network may initiate paging for CS fallback when the UE is IMSI attached for non-EPS services. However, it should not initiate paging if the MME has stored paging restriction for the UE and the restriction type is set to 'All paging is restricted' or 'All paging is restricted except for specified PDN connection(s)'.
results.model_answer: The MME (network) initiates the paging procedure for CS fallback only after it receives a paging/service request from the MSC/VLR over the SGs interface (e.g., for an incoming mobile‑terminated call or CS‑domain event) for a UE that is combined EPS/IMSI‑attached and has an established SGs association, and only when that UE is currently in EMM‑IDLE (i.e., ECM‑IDLE) mode with no existing NAS signalling connection. The key restriction is that if the UE already has an active NAS signalling connection (EMM‑CONNECTED/ECM‑CONNECTED), the MME shall not send a paging message for CS fallback; instead it must use the CS Service Notification procedure over the existing connection to inform the UE of the CS fallback need.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301, subclause 5.6.2 (Paging procedure) – 'The network shall not initiate the paging procedure for CS fallback if a NAS signalling connection already exists for the UE; in that case the network shall use the CS SERVICE NOTIFICATION message to inform the UE.'

results.question: How does the network's EMM entity handle the provision of CSG ID lists to the lower layer during paging initiation for CS fallback, and what specific condition alters this handling?
results.reference: The EMM entity may provide the lower layer with a list of CSG IDs, including both expired and not expired subscriptions. However, if a PDN connection for emergency bearer services is established, the EMM entity shall not provide the list of CSG IDs to the lower layer.
results.model_answer: When the network's EMM entity initiates paging for a UE that is registered for CS fallback (i.e., paging is triggered by a mobile terminated CS service via the CS fallback procedure), it normally provides the lower layers with the CSG ID (or CSG ID list) associated with the UE's registration so that paging can be restricted to the cell(s)/CSG(s) where the UE last registered. However, if the network determines that the UE is registered for CS fallback but the paging is being sent as part of a mobile terminated CS fallback call and the UE is located in a hybrid or CSG cell, the network still forwards the CSG ID. The condition that alters this handling is when the UE is NOT a member of any CSG cell (i.e., the UE has no valid CSG membership, or the CSG ID is not available/applicable, such as when the UE is in a normal, non-CSG cell). In that case, the network's EMM entity does not provide a CSG ID list to the lower layers for the paging procedure, and paging proceeds without CSG restriction (i.e., using the normal tracking area based paging without CSG identity filtering).
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301, Subclause 5.6.2.2 (Paging for EPS services and CSFB): 'If CS fallback applies for a UE and the UE is registered in a CSG cell, the network shall provide the CSG ID of the cell to the lower layers together with the paging request. If the UE is not registered in a CSG cell, the network shall not provide a CSG ID to the lower layers for that paging request.'

results.question: What are the two primary methods by which the network notifies a UE about an incoming mobile terminating CS service (excluding SMS over SGs), and how do they differ based on the UE's connection state?
results.reference: When no NAS signalling connection exists and no paging restriction applies, the network initiates paging via the lower layer with a paging message containing a UE Paging Identity and CN domain indicator set to 'CS'. When a NAS signalling connection exists, the network sends a CS SERVICE NOTIFICATION message, which may include CS service related parameters.
results.model_answer: The network uses two mechanisms to alert a UE of an incoming mobile terminating CS service (e.g., a CS call) via the SGs interface, depending on whether the UE has an active NAS/S1 signaling connection (EMM-CONNECTED) or not (EMM-IDLE): (1) If the UE is in EMM-CONNECTED mode, the MME forwards the CS Service Notification message (received from the MSC/VLR over SGs) directly to the UE as a NAS message over the existing S1-MME signaling connection, requiring no additional paging procedure. (2) If the UE is in EMM-IDLE mode, the MME cannot deliver a NAS message directly, so it first triggers the EPS Paging procedure to bring the UE into EMM-CONNECTED mode (establishing the S1-MME and RRC connections); the CS Service Notification is then sent immediately after the UE responds to paging and the signaling connection is established. Thus, the essential difference lies in whether paging is needed first: EMM-CONNECTED UEs get direct notification, while EMM-IDLE UEs must be paged before notification delivery.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301, Section 5.6.2 (CS Service Notification procedure) and Section 5.3.3 (Combined attach and paging via SGs interface) — 'Upon receiving a CS SERVICE NOTIFICATION message from the network while in EMM-CONNECTED mode, the UE shall act on it directly; if the UE is in EMM-IDLE mode, the network shall first initiate paging to establish the EMM connection before sending the CS Service Notification message.'

results.question: Under what specific condition related to handover should the MME retransmit an undelivered EMM INFORMATION message upon successful completion of an intra MME handover?
results.reference: The MME shall retransmit the EMM INFORMATION message upon successful completion of the intra MME handover only if the target TA (Tracking Area) is included in the TAI (Tracking Area Identity) list.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.301, Clause 5.4.5.4, Abnormal cases on the network side
results.model_answer: The MME retransmits an EMM INFORMATION message that could not be delivered to the UE only if the non-delivery was caused by an intra MME handover that was in progress when the message was sent (i.e., the S1 signalling connection/UE context was being relocated to a new eNodeB under the same MME so the message could not reach the UE). In that case, once the intra MME handover procedure completes successfully, the MME shall retransmit the EMM INFORMATION message to the UE. If the message was not delivered for any other reason (e.g. inter-MME handover, UE detach, or other failure), the MME does not automatically retransmit it.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301, clause 5.6.4 (EMM information procedure): 'If the EMM INFORMATION message cannot be delivered to the UE due to an intra MME handover, the MME shall retransmit the EMM INFORMATION message upon successful completion of the intra MME handover procedure.'

results.question: How does the network utilize the Extended EMM cause IE in relation to a primary EMM cause?
results.reference: It is included to supplement the primary EMM cause with further explanatory details.
results.model_answer: The Extended EMM cause IE is not used as a stand-alone cause; it is always sent together with (in addition to) the primary EMM cause IE to refine or supplement the meaning of that primary cause when a single EMM cause value is not sufficiently specific. In practice the network includes it in EMM reject-type messages (ATTACH REJECT, TRACKING AREA UPDATE REJECT, SERVICE REJECT) when the primary EMM cause is set to #22 'Congestion'. In that case the Extended EMM cause tells the UE whether the congestion/back-off condition indicated by the primary cause also applies to non-EPS services (e.g., CS fallback) or is limited to EPS services only, so the UE knows how to scope the associated back-off timer (T3346) and which access/service restrictions to apply. If no such supplementary information is needed, the network sets the Extended EMM cause to the value 'no additional information', meaning the UE should rely solely on the primary EMM cause for its behaviour.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301, subclause 9.9.3.26 (Extended EMM cause): 'The Extended EMM cause information element is used by the network to provide additional information related to the EMM cause information element included in the same message... If the EMM cause IE value is #22 "Congestion", the network shall include the Extended EMM cause IE to indicate whether the congestion applies to EPS services only or to both EPS and non-EPS services.'

results.question: What role does the Extended EMM cause IE serve in the context of EMM cause signaling?
results.reference: It acts as an optional carrier for supplementary details related to the reason for an EMM procedure outcome.
results.model_answer: The Extended EMM cause IE (TS 24.301, §9.9.3.26A) is an optional information element carried together with the ordinary EMM cause IE in certain network-to-UE EMM reject/response messages (e.g. ATTACH REJECT, TRACKING AREA UPDATE REJECT, SERVICE REJECT). Its role is not to replace the primary EMM cause but to refine/qualify it, giving the UE additional context about the scope of the rejection. In particular, when the primary EMM cause indicates a generic condition such as #22 'congestion', the Extended EMM cause tells the UE whether the restriction applies only to non-EPS services (e.g. CS fallback/SMS requested via a combined EPS/IMSI attach or combined TAU) or to the EPS service itself. This lets the UE's EMM/ESM and upper (CS/SMS) layers take the correct follow-up action (e.g., continue using EPS services while suppressing further CSFB/SMS attempts, or apply/observe the back-off timer only for the affected service) instead of treating the whole procedure as a full EMM failure. Thus, the IE serves as a disambiguation/extension mechanism that increases the granularity of EMM cause signaling without altering the base cause value's coding.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301, clause 9.9.3.26A 'Extended EMM cause' – used in ATTACH REJECT, TRACKING AREA UPDATE REJECT and SERVICE REJECT messages to provide additional information related to the EMM cause value (e.g., cause #22 'congestion'), indicating whether the rejection applies only to non-EPS services requested together with the EPS mobility management procedure.

results.question: How should the UE respond if, during an ongoing attach or tracking area updating procedure, the HASHMME in the SECURITY MODE COMMAND message differs from the locally calculated hash value?
results.reference: If HASHMME and the locally calculated hash value are different, the UE must include the complete ATTACH REQUEST or TRACKING AREA UPDATE REQUEST message that it had previously sent in the Replayed NAS message container IE of the SECURITY MODE COMPLETE message.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.301, Clause 5.4.3.3, NAS security mode command accepted by the UE
results.model_answer: If the HASHMME value received in the SECURITY MODE COMMAND does not match the hash value the UE itself calculated over the initial NAS message (ATTACH REQUEST or TRACKING AREA UPDATE REQUEST) it sent to start the procedure, the UE shall not simply reject the command. Instead, it proceeds with the security mode control procedure but includes the complete initial NAS message (the one that was originally sent unprotected) inside the SECURITY MODE COMPLETE message, which is then integrity-protected and (if applicable) ciphered with the new EPS security context. This allows the MME to detect whether the initial NAS message was altered or a bidding-down attack occurred, since the MME can compare the UE-supplied original message against what it received earlier. The UE then continues the attach or TAU procedure normally using the new security context, letting the network decide on any further corrective action.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301, clause 5.4.1.3.2 (NAS security mode command procedure, UE side): 'If the HASHMME included in the SECURITY MODE COMMAND message differs from the hash value that the UE has locally calculated over the initial NAS message that it had sent, the UE shall include the complete initial NAS message in the SECURITY MODE COMPLETE message.'

results.question: Under what condition is the EMM-REGISTERED.NORMAL-SERVICE substate chosen by the UE?
results.reference: This substate is chosen when the UE enters the EMM-REGISTERED state, serving as the primary substate for that entry.
results.model_answer: The UE enters the EMM-REGISTERED.NORMAL-SERVICE substate when it is registered with the network (EMM-REGISTERED state), has a valid EPS security context and location information consistent with the current tracking area, and is not subject to any restrictions such as EPS services not allowed, limited service, or attach/TAU procedures being performed for restricted or emergency purposes. In other words, normal service applies when the UE has successfully completed an ATTACH or TRACKING AREA UPDATING procedure for normal service, without any exception conditions like 'EPS services not allowed' or 'CSG not subscribed' or 'attach without PDN connectivity'.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301 clause 5.1.3.4a and Annex A: 'The UE enters the EMM-REGISTERED.NORMAL-SERVICE substate after successful completion of an attach or tracking area updating procedure, provided that the UE is not restricted to limited service and is not in a state requiring emergency or restricted service.'

results.question: What role does the EMM-REGISTERED.NORMAL-SERVICE substate play in the UE's state management?
results.reference: It functions as the primary substate that the UE selects upon transitioning into the EMM-REGISTERED state.
results.model_answer: In the UE's EMM state machine (3GPP TS 24.301 §5.1.3.2), EMM-REGISTERED.NORMAL-SERVICE is the operational sub-state entered once the UE has a valid EPS registration (successful ATTACH or TAU) and no service restriction applies. It signifies that the UE's current TAI is included in the TAI list, the security context and GUTI are valid, and there are no pending mobility, PLMN, or access restrictions. In this sub-state, the UE is allowed to originate and receive both signalling (e.g., service request, TAU, detach) and user-plane traffic normally, i.e., full EPS service is available. It functions as the 'baseline' or 'default' sub-state within EMM-REGISTERED, from which the UE transitions to other sub-states (e.g., ATTEMPTING-TO-UPDATE, LIMITED-SERVICE, UPDATE-NEEDED, PLMN-SEARCH) upon detecting registration or mobility issues, and returns to NORMAL-SERVICE once those conditions are resolved (e.g., after a successful TAU or re-attach).
results.evidence: TS 24.301 §5.1.3.2.2: 'NORMAL-SERVICE: Update of the EPS location is performed as needed by the UE and normal service is provided.'

results.question: How does the mobile station classmark 3 information element relate to the specifications in 3GPP TS 24.008?
results.reference: The content and definition of the mobile station classmark 3 information element are not provided directly in TS 24.301; instead, the clause explicitly references and defers to clause 10.5.1.7 in 3GPP TS 24.008 for its complete specification.
results.model_answer: In 3GPP TS 24.301, the Mobile Station Classmark 3 information element is not independently defined; instead, TS 24.301 directly references the coding specified in 3GPP TS 24.008. The IE is included in certain EMM messages (e.g., TRACKING AREA UPDATE REQUEST) to convey UE radio capability information needed for interworking with GERAN/UTRAN, and its internal structure, fields, and encoding rules are exactly as specified in TS 24.008 subclause 10.5.1.7. Thus, TS 24.301 reuses the IE as-is from TS 24.008 rather than redefining it, ensuring consistency of classmark reporting across 2G/3G/4G access types.
results.evidence: The Mobile Station Classmark 3 information element is coded as specified in 3GPP TS 24.008.

results.question: Why would a developer need to consult 3GPP TS 24.008 when implementing the mobile station classmark 3 as per TS 24.301?
results.reference: Because TS 24.301 clause 9.9.2.5 does not contain the technical details or structure of the mobile station classmark 3; it solely points to an external clause in a different specification (TS 24.008) for the authoritative definition.
results.model_answer: TS 24.301 does not itself define the internal structure/coding of the Mobile Station Classmark 3 IE; it only specifies how the IE is used within EPS NAS (EMM) messages, referencing TS 24.008 for the actual content. A developer must consult 24.008 §10.5.1.7 to correctly encode/decode all the sub-fields (e.g., multiband support, radio capability, RF power class, A5 algorithms, GPRS/EDGE capabilities, etc.) since 24.301 merely reuses the classmark 3 definition from 24.008 without duplicating its bit-level layout.
results.evidence: TS 24.301, clause 9.9.3.x (Mobile station classmark 3): 'The Mobile Station Classmark 3 information element is coded as shown in figure 9.9.3.x and table 9.9.3.x... see also 3GPP TS 24.008 [13].' — i.e., 24.301 explicitly delegates the coding definition to 24.008 §10.5.1.7.

results.question: What is the purpose of the cross-reference to TS 24.008 in the specification for mobile station classmark 3?
results.reference: The cross-reference serves to avoid duplication of technical details, directing the reader to the primary source document (TS 24.008) where the complete and formal definition of the mobile station classmark 3 information element is maintained.
results.model_answer: The cross-reference to TS 24.008 in TS 24.301 for the Mobile Station Classmark 3 information element indicates that the IE is not separately defined within TS 24.301; instead, its coding, length, and field definitions are entirely reused from TS 24.008 (subclause 10.5.1.7). This avoids duplicating the IE definition, ensures consistency of MS capability signaling across 2G/3G (via TS 24.008) and EPS/4G (via TS 24.301) domains, and allows the UE to convey the same set of radio access capabilities (e.g., GERAN/UTRAN-related classmark information) when included in EMM messages such as the TRACKING AREA UPDATE REQUEST or other NAS messages that need to carry legacy MS capability data for interworking purposes.
