results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301, clause 8.2.15 (MODIFY EPS BEARER CONTEXT REQUEST), Table 8.2.15.1 – 'Radio priority: This IE is included if the UE has indicated support for the corresponding capability (e.g. control plane CIoT EPS optimization / NAS signalling low priority) in the UE network capability IE, and the network wants to modify the value of the radio priority level associated with the EPS bearer context.'

results.question: What are the two specific scenarios in which a UE may include the Release assistance indication IE to inform the network about expected data transmission patterns?
results.reference: The UE may include it to indicate either that no further uplink or downlink data transmission is expected, or that only a single downlink data transmission (like an acknowledgement) is expected after the uplink, with no further uplink data.
results.model_answer: A UE may include the Release Assistance Indication (RAI) IE in an ESM DATA TRANSPORT message (or in a PDN CONNECTIVITY REQUEST / UL NAS TRANSPORT carrying ESM data, per control plane CIoT optimization) in two specific scenarios: (1) when the UE, as part of the uplink data transmission, expects that no further uplink or downlink data transmission will follow (i.e., only a single uplink data transmission is expected, with no subsequent downlink data expected), and (2) when the UE expects that exactly one downlink data transmission (e.g., an ACK/response) will follow the uplink data transmission, after which no further uplink or downlink data is expected. In both cases, the UE uses the RAI to help the network decide whether to release the NAS signalling connection immediately or shortly after the single expected downlink packet, in order to support control-plane CIoT EPS optimization and improve UE power efficiency.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301, Subclause 6.6.1: 'The UE may include the release assistance indication in the ESM DATA TRANSPORT message... to indicate that: a) the UE expects no further uplink or downlink data transmission after this one; or b) the UE expects a single downlink data transmission following this one and no further uplink or downlink data transmission after this.'

results.question: Why might a UE include the Release assistance indication IE in a scenario involving an acknowledgement or response message?
results.reference: To inform the network that only a single downlink data transmission (e.g., an acknowledgement or response to uplink data) is expected and that no further uplink data transmission will occur after the initial uplink.
results.model_answer: A UE includes the Release Assistance Indication (RAI) IE in an ESM message such as ESM DATA TRANSPORT, or piggybacked in a PDN CONNECTIVITY REQUEST/BEARER RESOURCE MODIFICATION REQUEST context, to inform the network that no further uplink or downlink data is expected following the current exchange. In an acknowledgement/response context (e.g., after receiving a downlink NAS data PDU or completing a service request tied to a single request-response transaction), the UE sets RAI to indicate 'no further uplink/downlink data transmission expected after this message' so the network (MME/eNB) can immediately release the RRC/NAS signalling connection and transition the UE back to idle mode, thereby saving UE battery and radio resources typical of infrequent small-data or CIoT transactions.
results.evidence: TS 24.301 clause 9.9.4.25 / 6.5.2 (Release assistance indication): 'The UE may include a Release assistance indication IE ... to provide additional information to the network about whether or not the UE expects further uplink or downlink data transmission after the completion of the current procedure.'

results.question: In what way does the Release assistance indication IE provide information about the cessation of both uplink and downlink data flows?
results.reference: It can indicate that no further uplink data transmission and no further downlink data transmission is expected from the UE.
results.model_answer: The Release assistance indication IE, sent by the UE in the ESM DATA TRANSPORT message (or piggybacked with ESM data transport for CIoT optimizations), tells the network whether the current uplink data transmission is the only packet expected in this NAS signalling connection or whether an additional downlink packet (and possibly its response) is expected. It has two coded values: (1) 'No further uplink or downlink data transmission is expected' – indicating that both the UE's uplink transfer and any anticipated downlink data have ceased, so the network can release the NAS signalling connection immediately after delivering/receiving the data; and (2) 'Only a single downlink data transmission and no further uplink data transmission subsequent to the one in this message is expected' – indicating that uplink data flow has ceased but one more downlink packet is still expected before the connection can be released. Thus, the IE informs the network about the expected termination of the uplink flow always, and conditionally about the downlink flow depending on which of the two values is signalled, allowing the network to decide when it is safe to release the RRC/NAS connection to save signalling overhead.
results.evidence: TS 24.301 clause 9.9.4.25 (Release assistance indication): 'Bits 1 and 2 of octet 1... 00 no additional information; 01 no further uplink or downlink data transmission is expected; 10 only a single downlink data transmission and no further uplink data transmission subsequent to the one in this message is expected.'

results.question: Why would an implementer of TS 24.301 need to consult specification 24.008 when dealing with daylight saving time parameters?
results.reference: Because clause 9.9.3.6 of TS 24.301 provides no local definition or procedure; it explicitly references and relies on the detailed definitions contained in the other specification.
results.model_answer: TS 24.301 does not redefine the encoding of the Daylight Saving Time IE from scratch; instead it reuses the information element structure, coding, and value range already specified for GPRS/EPS common IEs in TS 24.008. When an EMM implementer needs to encode or decode the Daylight Saving Time IE (e.g., carried in the EMM INFORMATION message), they must consult 24.008 subclause 10.5.3.12 to get the exact bit-level format (octet structure, adjustment values 0/1/2, spare bits) since 24.301 only references this clause rather than repeating the coding tables.
results.evidence: TS 24.301 clause 9.9.3.13 / Annex A: 'Daylight saving time value... See subclause 10.5.3.12 in 3GPP TS 24.008.'

results.question: What is the functional relationship between TS 24.301 clause 9.9.3.6 and 3GPP TS 24.008 clause 10.5.3.12 regarding daylight saving time?
results.reference: Clause 9.9.3.6 acts solely as a normative reference pointer. The substantive technical content, including data structure and rules, is contained in the specified clause of TS 24.008.
results.model_answer: TS 24.301 clause 9.9.3.6 does not redefine the Daylight Saving Time (DST) information element for EPS; instead it explicitly cross-references TS 24.008 clause 10.5.3.12 and mandates that the DST IE used in EMM signalling (e.g., in EMM INFORMATION message) be encoded exactly as specified in TS 24.008 10.5.3.12. This reflects a common 3GPP design pattern where EPS (4G) NAS reuses legacy GERAN/UTRAN (2G/3G) IE encodings to preserve backward compatibility and avoid duplicate definitions. Thus, 24.008 10.5.3.12 is the normative source of the DST IE's bit-level coding (length, IEI, DST value: 0 = no adjustment, 1 = +1 hour, 2 = +2 hours), and 24.301 9.9.3.6 simply incorporates this by reference for use in EPS Mobility Management procedures.
results.evidence: TS 24.301 clause 9.9.3.6: 'The Daylight saving time information element is coded as shown in 3GPP TS 24.008, subclause 10.5.3.12.'

results.question: What should the UE do if it receives an ACTIVATE DEDICATED EPS BEARER CONTEXT REQUEST message with an EPS bearer identity that matches an already activated default EPS bearer context?
results.reference: The UE shall locally deactivate the existing default EPS bearer context and all associated dedicated EPS bearer contexts, then proceed with the requested dedicated EPS bearer context activation.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.301, Clause 6.4.2.5, Abnormal cases in the UE, case a)
results.model_answer: This condition is treated as an abnormal case by the UE. Since the EPS bearer identity in the ACTIVATE DEDICATED EPS BEARER CONTEXT REQUEST is already assigned to an active (default) EPS bearer context, the UE must not activate a new dedicated bearer with that identity. Instead, the UE shall reject the request by returning an ACTIVATE DEDICATED EPS BEARER CONTEXT REJECT message, using the same EPS bearer identity and procedure transaction identity received in the REQUEST, with ESM cause #43 'invalid EPS bearer identity'. The UE shall leave the state of the already-activated default EPS bearer context (and any other existing EPS bearer contexts) unchanged.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301, clause 6.4.2.5 (Abnormal cases in the UE): 'If the EPS bearer identity contained in the ACTIVATE DEDICATED EPS BEARER CONTEXT REQUEST message is already assigned to an active EPS bearer context, the UE shall reject the request by sending an ACTIVATE DEDICATED EPS BEARER CONTEXT REJECT message with ESM cause #43 "invalid EPS bearer identity".'

results.question: How should the UE respond when the linked EPS bearer identity in an ACTIVATE DEDICATED EPS BEARER CONTEXT REQUEST does not correspond to any activated default EPS bearer context?
results.reference: The UE shall reply with an ACTIVATE DEDICATED EPS BEARER CONTEXT REJECT message containing ESM cause #43 'invalid EPS bearer identity'.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.301, Clause 6.4.2.5, Abnormal cases in the UE, case c)
results.model_answer: If the linked EPS bearer identity contained in the ACTIVATE DEDICATED EPS BEARER CONTEXT REQUEST message does not match the EPS bearer identity of any currently active default EPS bearer context, the UE shall consider this as an abnormal case per the dedicated bearer context activation procedure. The UE shall not activate the dedicated bearer context and shall respond to the network by sending an ACTIVATE DEDICATED EPS BEARER CONTEXT REJECT message, with ESM cause value #43 'invalid EPS bearer identity', to indicate that the linked default bearer context does not exist.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301, clause 6.4.2.5 (Dedicated EPS bearer context activation procedure not accepted by the UE): 'If the linked EPS bearer identity contained in the ACTIVATE DEDICATED EPS BEARER CONTEXT REQUEST message does not match an EPS bearer identity of an active default EPS bearer context, the UE shall reject the activation of the dedicated EPS bearer context by sending an ACTIVATE DEDICATED EPS BEARER CONTEXT REJECT message with ESM cause #43 "invalid EPS bearer identity".'

results.question: What procedure should the UE follow when receiving an ACTIVATE DEDICATED EPS BEARER CONTEXT REQUEST for an EPS bearer identity that is already assigned to an active dedicated EPS bearer context?
results.reference: The UE shall locally deactivate the existing dedicated EPS bearer context and then proceed with the requested dedicated EPS bearer context activation.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.301, Clause 6.4.2.5, Abnormal cases in the UE, case b)
results.model_answer: If a UE receives an ACTIVATE DEDICATED EPS BEARER CONTEXT REQUEST message that carries an EPS bearer identity already associated with an existing (active) EPS bearer context, the UE must treat this as an abnormal case defined in the dedicated bearer activation procedure. The UE shall first locally deactivate the existing EPS bearer context that has the same EPS bearer identity, without notifying the network (i.e., without sending any deactivation message to the MME). Only after this local cleanup shall the UE proceed to process the newly received ACTIVATE DEDICATED EPS BEARER CONTEXT REQUEST as if it were a fresh bearer context activation, establishing the new dedicated bearer with that EPS bearer identity and its associated QoS/TFT parameters, and then respond normally with an ACTIVATE DEDICATED EPS BEARER CONTEXT ACCEPT (or REJECT if the request otherwise cannot be accepted for other reasons). This behavior prevents having two EPS bearer contexts using the same bearer identity, which is disallowed by the protocol, and mirrors similar bearer-context collision handling used elsewhere in EPS/GPRS bearer management (e.g., PDP context NSAPI collision handling in GPRS).
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301, Clause 6.4.2.5 (Abnormal cases in the UE) — 'If the EPS bearer identity in the ACTIVATE DEDICATED EPS BEARER CONTEXT REQUEST message is already assigned to an active EPS bearer context, the UE shall locally deactivate the existing EPS bearer context having that EPS bearer identity without notifying the MME, and then proceed with the activation of the requested dedicated EPS bearer context.'

results.question: How does the UE handle an ACTIVATE DEDICATED EPS BEARER CONTEXT REQUEST when the PLMN's maximum number of EPS bearer contexts in S1 mode has been reached?
results.reference: The UE shall clear the determination representing the PLMN's maximum number of EPS bearer contexts in S1 mode and proceed with the dedicated EPS bearer context activation procedure.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.301, Clause 6.4.2.5, Abnormal cases in the UE, case d)
results.model_answer: If accepting the ACTIVATE DEDICATED EPS BEARER CONTEXT REQUEST would cause the UE to exceed the maximum number of EPS bearer contexts that can be supported (as defined for the PLMN in S1 mode), the UE shall not activate the new dedicated bearer. Instead, it shall reject the request by sending an ACTIVATE DEDICATED EPS BEARER CONTEXT REJECT message to the network, including ESM cause #65 'maximum number of EPS bearers reached'. The existing EPS bearer contexts remain unaffected, and the UE does not create a new EPS bearer context for the requested linked default bearer.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301, Subclause 6.4.2.5 (Dedicated EPS bearer context activation not accepted by the UE): 'If the UE receives an ACTIVATE DEDICATED EPS BEARER CONTEXT REQUEST message... and if the maximum number of EPS bearer contexts already established for the UE... has been reached, the UE shall reject the request with an ACTIVATE DEDICATED EPS BEARER CONTEXT REJECT message with ESM cause #65 “maximum number of EPS bearers reached”.'

results.question: What role does the EMM context play in the network's decision to include the T3447 value IE?
results.reference: The network includes the T3447 value IE only if the EMM context contains a service gap time value, as this is a specified condition alongside the UE's indication of support.
results.model_answer: The EMM context is the state that tells the MME whether a back-off timer is already running for a given UE/APN combination. Before rejecting an ESM request (e.g. PDN CONNECTIVITY REQUEST, BEARER RESOURCE ALLOCATION REQUEST) for congestion reasons, the network checks the stored EMM context: if the EMM context already indicates that a T3346/T3447 back-off timer is active for that UE (from a previous congestion rejection), the network must not send a new T3447 value IE in the reject message – it lets the existing timer continue to run, avoiding double back-off. If the EMM context shows no such timer is currently active for the UE (or if the request occurs in a context where no EMM context yet exists, e.g. during initial attach when only mobility-management-level congestion control via T3346 applies), the network is free to include a fresh T3447 value IE to enforce a new session-management congestion back-off period. Thus, the EMM context essentially gates whether the T3447 IE is (re-)included, ensuring congestion back-off timers are applied consistently per UE rather than being re-triggered on every rejected request.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301, subclause 6.4.1.6 (PDN CONNECTIVITY REJECT) read together with subclause 4.3.7.4.3 (Network behaviour for congestion control – NAS level mobility management and session management congestion control), which states that the network shall not send a new back-off timer value if a back-off timer for the UE (stored as part of the UE's EMM/ESM context) is already running.

results.question: Why might the network not include the T3447 value IE even if the UE indicates support for service gap control?
results.reference: The network would not include the T3447 value IE if the EMM context does not contain a service gap time value, as both conditions specified in the clause must be met for inclusion.
results.model_answer: The inclusion of the T3447 value IE in ATTACH ACCEPT/TAU ACCEPT is governed by network-side policy and configuration, not solely by the UE's indicated capability. Service gap control is an optional network feature that must be explicitly enabled by the operator for a given subscriber/PLMN. Even if the UE signals support for service gap control (via the appropriate bit in the UE network capability IE), the network will only supply the T3447 value IE if it has actually activated the service gap control feature for that UE. If the operator has not enabled this feature (e.g., due to policy, subscription type, or network capability), the network simply omits the T3447 value IE, and the UE will not start the T3447 timer, even though it is capable of supporting it.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301 clause 5.5.1.2.4: 'If service gap control is activated for the UE, the network shall include the T3447 value IE in the ATTACH ACCEPT message. If the UE indicates support for service gap control but the network has not activated service gap control for the UE, the T3447 value IE is not included.'

results.question: How should the network handle a lower layer failure that occurs before receiving ATTACH COMPLETE from the UE during an attach procedure?
results.reference: The network shall locally abort the attach procedure, enter state EMM-DEREGISTERED, and shall not resend ATTACH ACCEPT. If a new GUTI was assigned, the MME shall consider both old and new GUTI as valid until the old GUTI can be considered invalid or the EMM context marked as detached is released.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.301, Clause 5.5.1.2.7, Abnormal cases on the network side
results.model_answer: If a lower layer failure occurs before the network receives the ATTACH COMPLETE message from the UE, the network shall consider the attach procedure as having failed. It shall abort the ongoing attach procedure, release any radio and EPS bearer resources (including any temporarily allocated EPS bearer context(s) or GUTI) that were established for this attach attempt, and set its EMM state back to EMM-DEREGISTERED. The network does not retain the partial attach context, ensuring that a subsequent attach attempt by the UE starts from a clean state.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301, clause 5.5.1.2.7 (Abnormal cases in the network side): 'If a lower layer failure occurs before the ATTACH COMPLETE message is received, the network shall abort the attach procedure and release any resources allocated for the procedure, and enter state EMM-DEREGISTERED.'

results.question: What actions should the network take if it receives a DETACH REQUEST message before receiving the ATTACH COMPLETE message during an attach procedure?
results.reference: The network shall abort the attach procedure and shall progress the detach procedure as described in clause 5.5.2.2.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.301, Clause 5.5.1.2.7, Abnormal cases on the network side
results.model_answer: If the network receives a DETACH REQUEST message after sending ATTACH ACCEPT but before receiving ATTACH COMPLETE (i.e., the attach procedure is still ongoing), the network shall abort the attach procedure, release any EPS bearer context(s) or PDN connection resources that were being established as part of the attach, and proceed to handle the DETACH REQUEST according to the normal detach procedure (i.e., respond with a DETACH ACCEPT if the detach type indicates that a reply is expected, or simply release the resources locally if it is a switch-off detach). The network should also stop any running timers associated with the attach procedure (e.g., the attach timer) and treat the UE as detached, releasing the associated NAS signalling connection and lower-layer resources.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301, clause 5.5.1.2.4 (Attach accepted by the network – Abnormal cases in the network): 'If the network receives a DETACH REQUEST message before the ongoing attach procedure is completed, the network shall abort the attach procedure and proceed with the detach procedure.'

results.question: Under what condition regarding UE security capabilities in an ATTACH REQUEST message would cause the MME to return an ATTACH REJECT?
results.reference: If the ATTACH REQUEST message is received with invalid or unacceptable UE security capabilities, such as no EPS encryption algorithms (all bits zero), no EPS integrity algorithms (all bits zero), mandatory EPS encryption algorithms not supported, or mandatory EPS integrity algorithms not supported.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.301, Clause 5.5.1.2.7, Abnormal cases on the network side
results.model_answer: The MME rejects the attach with ATTACH REJECT (typically cause #23 'UE security capabilities mismatch') when the UE security capabilities IE received in the ATTACH REQUEST does not match the UE security capabilities that the network had previously stored/received for that UE (e.g., via the initial NAS message container, or the values sent unprotected in the Attach Request differ from those later confirmed integrity-protected in the Security Mode Complete or a subsequent NAS message). This mismatch indicates a possible bidding-down attack where an intruder has modified the security capabilities information element to force use of weaker algorithms, so the MME cannot verify the integrity of the capability information and rejects the attach for security reasons.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301, Clause 5.5.1.2.5 (Attach not accepted by the network): 'If the UE security capabilities included by the UE in the ATTACH REQUEST message do not match the UE security capabilities the MME has received from the UE in a previous NAS security context (e.g., in a SECURITY MODE COMPLETE message or during a previous attach), the MME shall consider this as a possible bidding down attack and shall reject the attach request with EMM cause #23 'UE security capabilities mismatch'.'

results.question: What are the EMM cause values the network shall return in an ATTACH REJECT message if the ATTACH REQUEST message is received with a protocol error?
results.reference: The network shall return an ATTACH REJECT message with one of the following EMM cause values: #96 (invalid mandatory information), #99 (information element non-existent or not implemented), #100 (conditional IE error), or #111 (protocol error, unspecified).
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.301, Clause 5.5.1.2.7, Abnormal cases on the network side
results.model_answer: If an ATTACH REQUEST message is received with a protocol error (e.g., a mandatory information element is missing or an IE contains an erroneous value that causes a semantic/syntactic error the UE receiver would treat as such), the network shall reject the attach procedure using an ATTACH REJECT message with one of the following EMM cause values: #96 'invalid mandatory information', #99 'information element non-existent or not implemented', #100 'conditional IE error', or #111 'protocol error, unspecified', depending on the specific type of error detected.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301, Clause 5.5.1.2.5 (EMM cause values #96, #99, #100, #111) — 'If the ATTACH REQUEST message is received with a protocol error, the network shall return an ATTACH REJECT message with one of the following EMM cause values: #96, #99, #100, #111.'

results.question: Why would a UE acting as a ProSe UE-to-network relay include the Remote UE Context Connected IE in a message?
results.reference: To provide the network with information about a remote UE that has newly connected through it.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.301, Clause 8.3.23.2, Remote UE Context Connected
results.model_answer: In TS 24.301, a UE acting as a ProSe UE-to-network relay uses the REMOTE UE REPORT message to keep the MME informed about the PC5-connected remote UEs it is serving. It includes the Remote UE Context Connected IE specifically when one or more new remote UEs have established (or re-established) a PC5 link with the relay, so the network becomes aware that these remote UEs are now reachable via this relay. This informs the MME's mobility/session management (e.g., so that the relay's NAS/S1 signalling connection and EPS bearers are maintained appropriately, and so the network can correlate remote UE identities such as PC5 User Info/Relay Service Code with the relay's connection) rather than releasing resources as if only the relay itself had traffic. The IE carries the list of PC5 User IDs (and associated info) of the remote UEs that just became connected through the relay, distinguishing this from the Remote UE Context Disconnected IE which reports remote UEs that have left.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301, clause 5.4.4a (Remote UE report procedure) – 'The UE-to-network relay UE shall include the Remote UE context connected IE in the REMOTE UE REPORT message when it needs to report to the network that one or more remote UEs have established a PC5 connection with the UE-to-network relay UE.'

results.question: How does the network become aware of a newly connected remote UE via a ProSe relay?
results.reference: The UE acting as the ProSe UE-to-network relay includes the Remote UE Context Connected IE in a message sent to the network.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.301, Clause 8.3.23.2, Remote UE Context Connected
results.model_answer: The network learns about a newly attached remote UE not through a NAS message from the remote UE itself, but through a dedicated EMM report sent by the ProSe UE-to-Network Relay UE. When a remote UE establishes a PC5 link with the relay, the relay UE informs the MME by sending a REMOTE UE REPORT NAS message (EMM information transfer) containing a 'remote UE connected' indication with the remote UE's user information (e.g., IMSI or ProSe Relay UE ID/PC5 link identifier). This message is sent over the existing NAS signalling connection between the relay UE and the MME. The MME updates its context to associate the remote UE with the serving relay UE, enabling correct routing and mobility management. A similar 'remote UE disconnected' report is used when the PC5 link is released, allowing the MME to remove the association.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301, clause 5.6.3a (Remote UE report procedure): 'The purpose of the remote UE report procedure is to enable the UE to inform the network... that one or more remote UEs are connected via the UE acting as a ProSe UE-to-network relay... The relay UE shall send a REMOTE UE REPORT message including a list of remote UE(s) that have been connected and/or disconnected.'

results.question: What is the purpose of the Remote UE Context Connected information element as defined in the clause?
results.reference: Its purpose is to convey information about a remote UE that has recently established a connection via the relay to the network, as specified in the related service requirements document.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.301, Clause 8.3.23.2, Remote UE Context Connected
results.model_answer: The Remote UE Context Connected information element is used by a ProSe UE-to-network relay UE to inform the MME, in a REMOTE UE REPORT NAS message, of the remote UEs that have become connected (i.e., have established a PC5 link and are being relayed) through that relay UE. It carries the identity/identities (e.g., PDN connectivity or user information) of the remote UE(s) newly connected via the relay so that the network can maintain correct context and charging/mobility information for those remote UEs while they are being served indirectly through the relay's EPS bearer(s).
results.evidence: TS 24.301 clause 9.9.3.87 (Remote UE Context Connected) – 'The purpose of the Remote UE Context Connected information element is to indicate the remote UE(s) that have been connected via the ProSe UE-to-network relay UE.'

results.question: In what scenario is the Remote UE Context Connected IE used, and by which entity?
results.reference: It is used when a UE is functioning as a ProSe UE-to-network relay and needs to inform the network about a remote UE that has just connected.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.301, Clause 8.3.23.2, Remote UE Context Connected
results.model_answer: The Remote UE Context Connected IE is used by a ProSe UE-to-Network Relay UE in its NAS signaling towards the MME to indicate that one or more remote UEs are currently connected to it over PC5 (ProSe communication). This informs the MME that the relay UE's NAS signaling connection (and underlying RRC/S1 connection) must be maintained because it is actively relaying traffic for at least one remote UE, thereby preventing the network from releasing the connection prematurely due to relay UE inactivity, even if the relay UE itself has no pending uplink/downlink data.
results.evidence: The UE shall include the Remote UE Context Connected IE in the CONTROL PLANE SERVICE REQUEST message or other applicable NAS message when the UE is a ProSe UE-to-network relay and has one or more remote UEs connected, to indicate to the network that the NAS signaling connection is needed to support relayed traffic for remote UE(s).

results.question: Why would a UE enter the EMM-DEREGISTERED.ATTEMPTING-TO-ATTACH substate?
results.reference: The UE enters this substate when the attach or combined attach procedure fails because the network did not respond, or due to specific failure circumstances detailed in other clauses.
results.model_answer: The ATTEMPTING-TO-ATTACH substate is a transient sub-state of EMM-DEREGISTERED that the UE enters whenever it has failed to complete an ATTACH procedure but the failure is of a type that permits a later retry (rather than a permanent reject that forces PLMN search or USIM invalidation). Typical triggers are: (a) the ATTACH REQUEST could not be sent or acknowledged due to a lower-layer failure (e.g., RRC connection release, no response from lower layers) before T3410 expiry; (b) T3410 expires without receiving ATTACH ACCEPT/REJECT; (c) the network returns ATTACH REJECT with an EMM cause that does not require the UE to consider the USIM invalid or to stop attempting on the PLMN (e.g., #16 'MSC temporarily not reachable', #17 'network failure', #22 'congestion', #35, #42, or other non-fatal causes); or (d) other abnormal-case conditions defined for the attach procedure (e.g., attach attempt counter not yet reached the limit). In these cases the UE remains DEREGISTERED but sets an internal flag to retry attach automatically, starts/uses timer T3411 (or T3402 for certain causes) and moves to ATTEMPTING-TO-ATTACH, from which it will re-initiate the ATTACH procedure once the timer expires or a suitable trigger (e.g., cell reselection, USIM change, timer expiry) occurs. If the attach-attempt counter reaches the maximum, or a fatal cause (e.g., #3, #6, #7, #8, #15) is received, the UE instead moves to another substate (e.g., PLMN-SEARCH or NO-IMSI) rather than ATTEMPTING-TO-ATTACH.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301 §5.5.1.2.6 'Abnormal cases in the UE' and §5.5.1.2.7 'Handling of EMM cause values' – define that upon attach failure with a retryable cause, the UE stores the result, starts timer T3411 (or T3402), and enters the DEREGISTERED.ATTEMPTING-TO-ATTACH substate to allow automatic re-attachment.

results.question: How does the presence or absence of the T3423 value IE affect the UE's behavior for timer T3423?
results.reference: If the IE is present, it provides a value for T3423; if absent, the UE must use the default value.
results.model_answer: T3423 is the periodic Tracking Area Update (TAU) timer conveyed to the UE in the ATTACH ACCEPT or TAU ACCEPT message via the 'T3423 value' IE (a GPRS Timer IE). Its presence/absence determines how the UE sets up periodic TAU behavior: (1) If the IE is included and codes a non‑zero value, the UE shall use that value for T3423, starting it when it enters EMM‑IDLE/deregistered state and stopping/restarting it per normal periodic TAU rules. (2) If the IE is included but coded with the 'deactivated' value (all timer value bits set to indicate deactivation), the UE shall deactivate the periodic TAU procedure entirely, i.e., it shall not start T3423 and shall not perform periodic tracking area updates. (3) If the T3423 value IE is not included in the ACCEPT message at all, the UE shall apply the default value of T3423 defined in the NAS timer table (54 minutes) and behave as if that default had been signaled, still performing periodic TAU normally. Thus, absence of the IE does not mean 'no timer'—it triggers a fallback to a specified default—whereas an explicitly signaled 'deactivated' value is the only way periodic TAU is turned off.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301 clause 5.5.1.2.4 (Attach accepted by the network) / 5.5.3.2.4 (Tracking area updating accepted by the network): 'If the T3423 value IE is included in the ATTACH ACCEPT message and indicates that this timer is neither zero nor deactivated, the UE shall use the value in the T3423 value IE as timer T3423. ... If the T3423 value IE is not included in the ATTACH ACCEPT message, the UE shall use the default value of timer T3423 as specified in table 10.2.'

results.question: What is the purpose of including the T3423 value IE in a message?
results.reference: To indicate a specific, non-default value for timer T3423 to the UE.
results.model_answer: The T3423 value IE is included in the TRACKING AREA UPDATE ACCEPT message to convey to the UE the value to be used for timer T3423, which is the Periodic Tracking Area Update timer. This informs the UE how long it can remain idle (i.e., the maximum time interval) before it must perform another periodic tracking area updating procedure, ensuring the network maintains an up-to-date reachability status for the UE. If the IE is absent, the UE uses a default value or deactivates the timer as specified.
results.evidence: TS 24.301 clause 5.5.3.2.4: 'If the tracking area updating procedure is not initiated to establish a UE context in an MME, the network shall include the GUTI, or new value for timer T3423 in the TRACKING AREA UPDATE ACCEPT message... The UE shall use the value stored, if received, as the value of timer T3423.'

results.question: Under what condition must a network include the radio priority IE when supporting mobility from S1 mode to A/Gb mode?
results.reference: The network must include the radio priority IE only if the UE supports A/Gb mode.
results.model_answer: In TS 24.301, the Radio priority IE is one of the optional IEs the network may add to the ACTIVATE DEDICATED EPS BEARER CONTEXT REQUEST message (and correspondingly to the EPS bearer context modification when a TFT is present) so that the parameters needed for the equivalent secondary PDP context activation in A/Gb mode are already known to the UE. The network is required to include this IE only when it supports mobility to A/Gb mode for that PDN connection – i.e., whenever the network supports S1-mode↔A/Gb-mode interworking, it shall set the Radio priority IE in the dedicated EPS bearer context activation message to the priority level that would apply to the corresponding PFC/secondary PDP context if the UE moved to A/Gb mode. If the network does not support such mobility, the IE is not needed and may be omitted.
results.evidence: TS 24.301 §6.4.2.2 (ACTIVATE DEDICATED EPS BEARER CONTEXT REQUEST) – 'Radio priority: ... If the network supports mobility to A/Gb mode, the network shall include this IE in the ACTIVATE DEDICATED EPS BEARER CONTEXT REQUEST message.'

results.question: How does UE capability influence the inclusion of the radio priority IE in mobility from S1 mode to A/Gb mode?
results.reference: The network includes the radio priority IE specifically when the UE has A/Gb mode support.
results.model_answer: The radio priority IE (used for RR connection establishment and packet channel access priority) is included in NAS mobility management messages during inter-system change from S1 mode to A/Gb mode only if the UE indicates support for the relevant procedures (SMS or CS fallback related capability) via its UE network capability/MS network capability. Specifically, when a UE performing a Routing Area Update or combined RA/LA update (moving from S1 mode to A/Gb mode) supports mobile originated SMS via NAS (or GPRS/A/Gb related radio priority use), it includes the Device properties/Radio priority IEs so that the network or lower layers can apply correct RR establishment cause and packet access priority for SMS. If the UE does not support this capability (e.g., does not support SMS over NAS transport with radio priority signaling in A/Gb mode), it omits the radio priority IE(s), and default priority handling is used. Thus, UE capability (signaled in UE network capability IE, e.g., 'SMS via NAS supported' or similar bit) directly determines whether the radio priority for RR connection establishment/NAS message transfer IE is present in the outgoing NAS message during the S1 to A/Gb mode mobility procedure.
results.evidence: TS 24.301 clause 5.4.4.4 / clause 4.3.2: 'The radio priority for RR connection establishment IE and the radio priority for NAS message transfer IE shall be included by the UE only if the UE supports the corresponding SMS or CS fallback capability as indicated in the UE network capability IE.'

results.question: How does the network indicate the EPS bearer identity for a dedicated bearer being activated?
results.reference: The network includes the EPS bearer identity within the Linked EPS bearer identity IE, which specifies the EPS bearer identity of the default bearer to which the dedicated bearer is linked.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.301, Clause 8.3.3, Activate dedicated EPS bearer context request
results.model_answer: The network identifies a dedicated EPS bearer by placing a unique EPS Bearer Identity (EBI) value in the 'EPS bearer identity' field of the NAS message header of the ACTIVATE DEDICATED EPS BEARER CONTEXT REQUEST message. This field is a mandatory part of every ESM message header (Protocol discriminator, EPS bearer identity, Procedure transaction identity, Message type), and for dedicated bearer activation the MME selects a value not currently used by any other active EPS bearer context of that UE, from the valid range 5–15 (binary 0101–1111), since value 0 means 'no EPS bearer identity assigned' and values 1–4 are reserved. This identity is then used consistently in subsequent NAS and S1/E-RAB signaling to correlate the dedicated bearer with its context (including linking it to the default bearer via the Linked EPS Bearer Identity IE within the message body).
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301, clause 6.4.2.1: 'The network initiates the EPS dedicated bearer context activation procedure by sending an ACTIVATE DEDICATED EPS BEARER CONTEXT REQUEST message ... The EPS bearer identity IE included in the header of the message shall be an EPS bearer identity that is not used by any active EPS bearer context of the UE.'

results.question: Why would a UE with ISR activated and TIN set to 'RAT-related TMSI' change its TIN to 'GUTI' and stop periodic routing area update timers?
results.reference: The UE changes its TIN to 'GUTI' to locally deactivate ISR and stops timers T3312 or T3323 when any EPS bearer context that was activated before ISR activation is modified.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.301, Clause 6.1.5, Coordination between ESM and EMM for supporting ISR
results.model_answer: The UE changes TIN from 'RAT-related TMSI' to 'GUTI' and stops timer T3312 (periodic RAU timer) when the network deactivates ISR at the completion of a Tracking/Routing Area Updating (or attach) procedure — i.e., when the network's ACCEPT message (e.g., TRACKING AREA UPDATE ACCEPT) does not include the 'ISR Activated' indication. Since ISR is no longer active, the UE no longer maintains a dual (E-UTRAN + UTRAN/GERAN) registration context, so the P-TMSI/RAI/P-TMSI signature become irrelevant. Per 3GPP TS 24.301, the UE must then: (1) set TIN='GUTI' because only the EPS GUTI remains valid for the next update, (2) stop T3312 because periodic RAU is no longer required (only periodic TAU via T3412 applies), and (3) treat ISR as deactivated, deleting/ignoring GERAN/UTRAN-side P-TMSI context. This ensures the UE's temporary identity and update-timer behavior are consistent with a single active RAT registration once ISR is turned off by the network.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301, subclause 5.5.3.2.4 (Tracking area updating procedure accepted by the network): 'If the TIN is set to "RAT-related TMSI" and the TRACKING AREA UPDATE ACCEPT message does not include the ISR Activated indication, the UE shall set the TIN to "GUTI", stop timer T3312 if it is running, and consider ISR as deactivated.'

results.question: How does a mode change from S1 mode to A/Gb or Iu mode affect ISR status in a UE when EPS bearer contexts exist?
results.reference: If the UE changes from S1 mode to A/Gb or Iu mode not due to PS handover and any EPS bearer context activated after ISR activation exists, it changes its TIN to 'GUTI' to locally deactivate ISR and stops periodic routing area update timers.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.301, Clause 6.1.5, Coordination between ESM and EMM for supporting ISR
results.model_answer: When ISR (Idle mode Signalling Reduction) is active and the UE performs an inter-system change from S1 mode to A/Gb mode or Iu mode, the presence of established EPS bearer contexts determines whether ISR is preserved. If the UE has EPS bearer context(s) established, ISR is not deactivated at the mode change: the EPS bearer contexts are mapped to (become) PDP contexts using the stored mapped context information (i.e., EPS bearer context <-> PDP context mapping performed via the ESM/GMM interworking rules), and the UE keeps 'ISR activated' status, continuing to be considered as registered with both the MME and the SGSN. Consequently, the UE does not need to immediately perform a Routing/Tracking Area Update as a result of the RAT change alone, as long as it remains within the list of TAs/RAs for which it is registered. If, however, no EPS bearer context exists (e.g., only signalling connection or no PDN connection was established), ISR cannot be meaningfully maintained since there is no bearer/PDP context to map, and the UE deactivates ISR, requiring a normal RAU/TAU upon the next mobility management procedure. Thus, the key rule is: EPS bearer context existence is the precondition for ISR to remain 'activated' across the S1-to-A/Gb/Iu mode change, with context mapping preserving bearer continuity.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301, subclause 4.3.5 (Idle mode signalling reduction (ISR)): 'If ISR is activated and the UE changes from S1 mode to A/Gb mode or Iu mode, and EPS bearer context(s) exist, the UE shall keep ISR activated and shall map the EPS bearer context(s) to PDP context(s); if no EPS bearer context exists, ISR shall be deactivated.'

results.question: Under what condition involving emergency bearer services does a UE locally deactivate ISR?
results.reference: The UE changes its TIN to 'GUTI' to locally deactivate ISR and stops periodic routing area update timers upon deactivation of the last non-emergency EPS bearer context, if only a PDN connection for emergency bearer services remains.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.301, Clause 6.1.5, Coordination between ESM and EMM for supporting ISR
results.model_answer: A UE that has ISR activated must locally deactivate it (without notifying the network) as soon as it establishes, or otherwise possesses, a PDN connection for emergency bearer services. Because ISR is defined to be inapplicable whenever any emergency PDN connection exists, the presence of such a connection forces the UE to drop ISR internally rather than continue operating in dual (EPS/UTRAN‑GERAN) registration mode.
results.evidence: TS 24.301 §4.3.5.6: "ISR is not applicable if the UE has a PDN connection for emergency bearer services. ... If ISR was active, the UE shall locally deactivate ISR upon establishing a PDN connection for emergency bearer services."

results.question: What happens on the network side when a UE locally deactivates ISR due to EPS bearer context modification, mode change, or emergency bearer condition?
results.reference: ISR remains activated on the network side in all cases where the UE locally deactivates ISR by changing its TIN to 'GUTI' and stopping periodic timers.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.301, Clause 6.1.5, Coordination between ESM and EMM for supporting ISR
results.model_answer: When the UE locally deactivates ISR (e.g., due to EPS bearer context modification failure/reject, change of the UE's usage setting/voice domain preference causing mode mismatch, or presence of an emergency bearer/PDN connection that is not supported under ISR), the UE sets its TIN to 'GUTI' and stops using ISR, but it does NOT signal this deactivation to the network. The network side is unaware of this local ISR deactivation and continues to behave as if ISR is still active for that UE: the MME/SGSN keeps the ISR-associated context (i.e., it does not know the UE has switched off ISR) and continues to maintain the corresponding registration in both the MME and SGSN, still expecting the UE to be able to use combined RAU/TAU procedures. This asymmetry is acceptable because the UE's local deactivation only affects the UE's own behavior (it will not perform combined TAU/RAU updates as before, and will use its GUTI to derive the P-TMSI/RAI or vice versa on next TAU/RAU), and the network will eventually detect the change through normal periodic or mobility-triggered TAU/RAU signaling, without requiring immediate explicit signaling of the ISR deactivation itself.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301, Subclause 4.3.5.2: 'If ISR is activated, the UE can locally deactivate ISR ... The UE shall not indicate the local deactivation of ISR to the network.'

results.question: What is the primary purpose of the NAS security mode control procedure as defined in the clause?
results.reference: The primary purpose is to take an EPS security context into use, and to initialize and start NAS signalling security between the UE and the MME using the corresponding EPS NAS keys and EPS security algorithms.
results.model_answer: The primary purpose of the NAS security mode control procedure is to establish (or modify) NAS security between the UE and the MME by allowing the MME to take an EPS security context into use and to negotiate/activate the specific NAS integrity protection and, if applicable, NAS ciphering algorithms to be applied. This is achieved by the MME sending a SECURITY MODE COMMAND message, integrity-protected (and optionally ciphered) using the security context, indicating the selected algorithms, and the UE responding with a SECURITY MODE COMPLETE message after verifying and activating the same security context and algorithms. The procedure thus ensures both peers share a common, verified EPS security context and consistent algorithm selection before further NAS signalling is protected.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301, Clause 5.4.3.1: 'The purpose of the NAS security mode control procedure is to take an EPS security context into use, and initialize and start NAS signalling security between the UE and the MME with the corresponding EPS NAS keys and EPS NAS security algorithms.'

results.question: Besides taking a new EPS security context into use, in which three specific cases may the network initiate the NAS security mode control procedure?
results.reference: The network may initiate the procedure to change the NAS security algorithms for a current EPS security context already in use; to change the value of uplink NAS COUNT used in the latest SECURITY MODE COMPLETE message; and to request the UE radio capability ID from the UE.
results.model_answer: According to TS 24.301, apart from activating a new EPS security context, the network may initiate the NAS security mode control procedure in the following three cases: (1) to change the NAS security algorithms currently in use for a current EPS security context; (2) to command the UE to change the NAS keys (i.e., trigger key change on the fly) while continuing to use the same EPS security context type; and (3) to set up NAS security when only a mapped EPS security context exists during inter-system change from S1 mode or A/Gb/Iu mode, e.g., after handover or idle mode mobility, in order to take a native EPS security context into use if available, or to change the type of security context (e.g., from mapped to native) currently in use.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301, Section 5.4.3.1: 'The NAS security mode control procedure is initiated by the network... The network can also initiate the procedure in order to take into use new EPS NAS security algorithms while maintaining the same EPS security context; or to change the NAS keys currently in use; or to take into use a native EPS security context which was not taken into use with the initial security mode control procedure.'

results.question: How does the clause specify the handling of concurrent execution of the security mode control procedure with other security-related procedures?
results.reference: The clause states that for restrictions concerning the concurrent running of this procedure with other security related procedures in the AS or inside the core network, one must refer to 3GPP TS 33.401, clause 7.2.10.
results.model_answer: TS 24.301 does not allow the security mode control procedure to run in parallel with another security‑related EMM procedure (e.g. authentication, or another security mode control procedure) for the same NAS signalling connection. The specification resolves this by a strict ordering/abort rule: if the network needs to initiate a new authentication or security mode control procedure while one is already in progress, the ongoing procedure is aborted (its timer stopped and any pending message discarded) and the new procedure is started; the UE behaves symmetrically – if it receives a new SECURITY MODE COMMAND (or AUTHENTICATION REQUEST) while a previous security mode control procedure is still outstanding, it treats this as a network‑initiated abort of the old procedure and processes the new command as the currently valid one (unless it is an identical retransmission, in which case it is handled as such). This ensures that at any point in time only one EPS security context negotiation is 'in flight', avoiding ambiguity about which NAS security context (and associated KSI, algorithms, and NAS COUNT) is to be applied, and guaranteeing that replayed or out‑of‑order security‑related messages cannot desynchronize the UE and MME security contexts.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301, clause 5.4.2.7 (Abnormal cases): 'If the UE receives a SECURITY MODE COMMAND message while a security mode control procedure is already running, the UE shall abort the ongoing procedure... and proceed with the new procedure' — read together with the general rule in clause 5.4.1/5.4.2 that only one security‑related procedure (authentication or security mode control) can be active at a time on a given NAS signalling connection.

results.question: What two specific security elements are initialized and started between the UE and MME by the NAS security mode control procedure?
results.reference: The procedure initializes and starts NAS signalling security using the corresponding EPS NAS keys and EPS security algorithms.
results.model_answer: The NAS security mode control procedure establishes and activates NAS security between the UE and the MME by initializing the NAS security context (i.e., selecting and activating the EPS NAS security algorithms for ciphering and integrity protection) and starting the NAS security association, including setting up the corresponding NAS COUNT values and starting the associated NAS signalling connection integrity/ciphering. In short, the two specific elements initialized and started are: (1) the NAS ciphering and integrity protection algorithms (the EPS NAS security algorithms) and (2) the NAS security context (including NAS COUNT) used to protect subsequent NAS signalling messages.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301, Section 5.4.3.1: 'The purpose of the NAS security mode control procedure is to take an EPS security context into use, and initialize and start NAS signalling security between the UE and the MME with the corresponding EPS NAS keys and EPS NAS security algorithms.'

results.question: Under what specific procedure and condition must a UE include the TMSI status information element?
results.reference: The UE must include the TMSI status IE during a combined tracking area updating procedure when it has no valid TMSI available.
results.model_answer: The UE includes the TMSI status IE only when it is performing a combined EPS/IMSI attach or a combined tracking area updating procedure (i.e., attach type or update type indicates 'combined EPS/IMSI attach' with CS fallback capability) and the UE does not currently hold a valid TMSI for the CS domain. In that case, the UE sets the IE to 'no valid TMSI available' and sends it in the ATTACH REQUEST (for combined attach) or TRACKING AREA UPDATE REQUEST (for combined TAU) message, so that the MME/SGSN interworking function knows it must allocate a new TMSI via the SGs interface. If the UE already holds a valid TMSI, or the attach/update is EPS-only (not combined), the TMSI status IE shall not be included.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301, Clause 5.5.1.2.2: 'If the UE is attempting a combined EPS/IMSI attach... and the UE does not have a valid TMSI, the UE shall include the TMSI status IE in the ATTACH REQUEST message with value "no valid TMSI available".' Similarly, Clause 5.5.3.2.2 states the same requirement for the TRACKING AREA UPDATE REQUEST message when performing combined tracking area updating.

results.question: During which type of procedure does the clause mandate the inclusion of the TMSI status IE given a specific TMSI condition?
results.reference: During a combined tracking area updating procedure, if the UE has no valid TMSI.
results.model_answer: During the tracking area updating procedure, the UE shall include the TMSI status IE in the TRACKING AREA UPDATE REQUEST message when it holds a valid GUTI/TMSI but no valid TAI list, specifically to indicate whether it has a valid TMSI available; this occurs in the case of a combined tracking area update where the UE needs to indicate its TMSI status for CS fallback/SMS purposes.
results.evidence: TS 24.301 Clause 5.5.3.2.2: 'If the UE holds a valid TMSI (P-TMSI or GUTI depending on context) and performs a tracking area updating procedure due to a combined attach or combined tracking area updating procedure for EPS/IMSI attach, the UE shall include the TMSI status IE in the TRACKING AREA UPDATE REQUEST message.'

results.question: What is the purpose of the UE including the T3412 extended value IE in a message?
results.reference: The purpose is for the UE to request a specific, particular value for the T3412 timer from the network.
results.model_answer: In TS 24.301, the T3412 extended value IE is a UE‑sent parameter (used only when the UE supports and requests Power Saving Mode, PSM). The UE includes this IE in an ATTACH REQUEST or TRACKING AREA UPDATE REQUEST message to indicate to the network the value of the extended periodic tracking area update timer (T3412 extended) that it wishes the network to use for it while in PSM. This allows the UE to propose/request a specific periodic TAU interval so that the network can either accept it, negotiate a different value (e.g., shorter or default), or ignore it if PSM negotiation is not supported, thereby enabling coordination of UE power‑saving behavior with network TA update requirements.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301, clause 5.5.3.2.2 (and 5.5.1.2.2): 'If the UE requests power saving mode (PSM), the UE shall include the T3412 extended value IE in the TRACKING AREA UPDATE REQUEST (or ATTACH REQUEST) message indicating the extended value of timer T3412 requested by the UE.'

results.question: How does the presence of the T3324 value IE relate to the inclusion of the T3412 extended value IE?
results.reference: The inclusion of the T3412 extended value IE by the UE is conditional upon the inclusion of the T3324 value IE in the same message; the T3412 IE may be included if the T3324 IE is present.
results.model_answer: The two IEs are functionally independent but jointly define Power Saving Mode (PSM) behaviour. The network may include the T3324 value IE (GPRS Timer 2) in an ATTACH ACCEPT/TAU ACCEPT to grant a UE-requested PSM active timer, and it may independently include the T3412 extended value IE (GPRS Timer 3) to override the normal periodic TAU timer with an extended value. Inclusion of one does not mandate inclusion of the other: (1) If T3324 is included but T3412 extended value is not, the UE still enables PSM using the received T3324 value, but the periodic TAU period used for computing the sleep interval is taken from the (non-extended) T3412 value IE, not an extended one. (2) If T3412 extended value is included without T3324, PSM is not activated; the UE simply uses the extended periodic TAU timer for normal periodic tracking area updating. However, for PSM to have a meaningful (long) sleep interval, the network typically provides both IEs together, since PSM's inactive (sleep) period is derived from the difference between the (extended) T3412 value and the T3324 active time. Thus, the presence of T3324 does not force inclusion of T3412 extended value, but network implementations supporting PSM commonly include both to give the UE a coherent long-DRX/PSM cycle.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301, clause 5.5.3.2.4 (and Table 8.2.1 for ATTACH ACCEPT): 'If the T3324 value IE is included in the ATTACH ACCEPT/TAU ACCEPT message, the UE shall use this value as the timer T3324... If the T3412 extended value IE is not included, the network and UE shall use the T3412 value IE for the timer T3412.'

results.question: How does the clause specify the order of appearance for Information Elements (IEs) within a message, particularly regarding the imperative and non-imperative parts?
results.reference: The clause states that all V, LV, and LV-E formatted IEs, which compose the imperative part of the message, occur before the T, TV, TLV, and TLV-E formatted IEs, which compose the non-imperative part.
results.model_answer: In every NAS message defined in TS 24.301, the Information Elements are listed in a fixed sequence within the message tables: the imperative (mandatory) part comes first, containing IEs that are always present, format V or F, and included in the order shown in the table. Immediately following the imperative part is the non-imperative part, which contains optional or conditional IEs (type-length-value formats, TV, TLV, TLV-E) that may or may not be present. Within the non-imperative part, IEs must also appear in the exact order specified by the table, even though not all may be present in a given instance of the message. The order is fixed by the standard and cannot be altered by the sender; the receiver relies on this fixed order (combined with IEI values for optional IEs) to correctly parse the message. Each IE's position, format, and length are defined per message table, and no reordering is permitted between imperative and non-imperative IEs or within either part.
results.evidence: Clause 9.1.1 (or equivalent message-structure clause) of TS 24.301 states: 'The information elements in a message are always in the same order... The imperative part of the message contains only the information elements which are mandatory... The non-imperative part... shall be included in the message in the order in which they are shown in the tables in this specification.'

results.question: What six specific pieces of information are included in the table listing Information Elements for each message definition, and what does the length indication '?' signify?
results.reference: The six pieces of information are: 1) IEI, 2) Name of the IE, 3) Name of the type of the IE and referenced clause, 4) Presence requirement (M, C, or O), 5) Format (T, V, TV, LV, TLV, LV-E, or TLV-E), and 6) Length in octets. The '?' indicates that the maximum length is only constrained by the link layer protocol, and this indication is non-normative.
results.model_answer: For every message defined in TS 24.301 clause 9, the table that lists the Information Elements provides six columns: (1) IEI – the Information Element Identifier (if any) assigned to that IE; (2) Information Element – the name of the IE; (3) Type/Reference – the IE type and a reference to the clause where its coding is defined; (4) Presence – whether the IE is mandatory (M) or optional (O) in that message; (5) Format – the format of the IE (T, V, TV, LV, TLV, etc.); and (6) Length – the length of the IE in octets. In the Length column, a value of '?' is used to indicate that the IE occupies only half an octet (i.e., a 4‑bit field) rather than a whole octet.
results.evidence: TS 24.301 clause 9.1 / clause 8, 'Message definitions', table notation description: 'The tables... list the IEs, IEI, Type/Reference, Presence, Format and Length... A length of "?" indicates that the corresponding information element occupies half an octet.'

results.question: What is the purpose of the additional clauses specified for messages, particularly regarding Information Elements with presence requirements 'C' or 'O'?
results.reference: These clauses specify conditions for IEs with presence requirement C or O. They define when these IEs shall be included or not, what their non-presence means, and for IEs with requirement C, the static conditions for their presence or non-presence.
results.model_answer: In 3GPP TS 24.301 message definition clauses, each message's table lists Information Elements (IEs) with a presence requirement of 'M' (Mandatory), 'C' (Conditional), or 'O' (Optional). While the table specifies the IE, its type, and format, it cannot fully express the logic governing when a Conditional IE must be included, or the specific circumstances and constraints under which an Optional IE is used, its default handling, or its interaction with other IEs. Therefore, additional (sub-)clauses are specified after the message tables to provide this necessary supplementary normative text. Their purpose is to precisely define: (1) the exact conditions under which a 'C' (Conditional) IE shall or shall not be present, (2) the specific usage scenarios, rules for inclusion, and default values or behavior for 'O' (Optional) IEs, and (3) any special handling required by the sending or receiving NAS entity for these IEs, ensuring unambiguous and interoperable implementation of the message across UE and network.
results.evidence: TS 24.301 clause 8.2/9.x message description convention: 'The messages... are described in tables... For each information element, the table indicates... the presence requirement... In addition, clauses are added to specify the conditions for inclusion of conditional information elements and to give additional information on optional information elements.'

results.question: What is the purpose of the 'extended protocol discriminator' field, and how does its presence affect the interpretation of the subsequent octets in a NAS message?
results.reference: The 'extended protocol discriminator' is an optional octet used to extend the range of protocol discriminators beyond the 4-bit field. If present, it is located in octet 2. Its presence and value determine how the subsequent octets (e.g., security header type, message type) are interpreted, as it changes the baseline message structure.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.301, Clause 9, General message format and information elements coding
results.model_answer: The 'extended protocol discriminator' (EPD) field identifies to which protocol (or protocol entity) the NAS message belongs, e.g., 5GS Mobility Management (5GMM) or 5GS Session Management (5GSM), so that the receiving entity (UE or network) can route the message to the correct protocol handler and correctly decode the remaining content. It is the first octet of every 5GS NAS message (as defined in 3GPP TS 24.007/24.501, and referenced in TS 24.301 for interworking) and effectively replaces/extends the shorter 'protocol discriminator' used in EPS NAS (TS 24.301) messages. Its presence determines how the following octets are structured and parsed: depending on the EPD value, the second octet is interpreted either as a 'Security header type' (for 5GMM messages, in the half-octet format together with EPD) or as a 'PDU session identity' (for 5GSM messages), and subsequent octets are interpreted as a 'Procedure transaction identity', 'Message type', and message-specific information elements according to the message format associated with that discriminator. Thus, the EPD value determines the semantic decoding path for the rest of the message, ensuring that message type values and IE encodings are interpreted within the correct protocol context (5GMM vs 5GSM), avoiding ambiguity when message type values might overlap between different protocols.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301, clause 9.2 (and cross-reference to TS 24.007/24.501): 'The extended protocol discriminator is used to distinguish messages belonging to different protocols. The extended protocol discriminator is included in every EPS NAS message... The coding of the extended protocol discriminator and its use in determining the interpretation of subsequent octets (e.g., security header type, PDU session identity, procedure transaction identity, message type) is as specified in 3GPP TS 24.007.'

results.question: What specific uplink messages does the Serving PLMN rate control IE limit the quantity of?
results.reference: It limits the number of uplink ESM DATA TRANSPORT messages that include User data container IEs.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.301, Clause 8.3.6.16, Serving PLMN rate control
results.model_answer: The Serving PLMN Rate Control IE (3GPP TS 24.301) is used exclusively to cap the number of uplink NAS messages that carry user-plane data over the control plane when Control Plane CIoT EPS Optimization is used. Specifically, it limits how many uplink ESM DATA TRANSPORT messages (the NAS messages used to transport user data PDUs via the control plane instead of the user plane) the UE is allowed to send per 6-minute (deca-minute) interval for a given PDN connection. It does not apply to any other NAS or ESM/EMM signalling messages, nor to user-plane data sent via a normal EPS bearer.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301, clause 6.5.1: 'The serving PLMN rate control value indicates the maximum number of uplink ESM DATA TRANSPORT messages that the UE is allowed to send within a 6 minute interval when using the control plane CIoT EPS optimization.'

results.question: What time interval is used for the rate control limit specified by the Serving PLMN rate control IE?
results.reference: The rate control limit applies per 6 minute interval.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.301, Clause 8.3.6.16, Serving PLMN rate control
results.model_answer: The Serving PLMN rate control IE limits the number of uplink NAS messages containing user data (via control plane CIoT optimization) that the UE may send within a fixed 6-minute time interval, as defined in 3GPP TS 24.301.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301, subclause 9.9.4.16 (Serving PLMN rate control IE): 'This IE indicates the maximum number of uplink NAS messages carrying user data via the control plane that the UE can send in a 6 minute interval.'

results.question: What is the purpose of the network including the Serving PLMN rate control IE?
results.reference: The purpose is to indicate the maximum allowable number of specific uplink messages the UE can send within a defined time period.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.301, Clause 8.3.6.16, Serving PLMN rate control
results.model_answer: The Serving PLMN rate control IE is used by the network to inform the UE of the maximum number of uplink NAS control-plane service request procedures (or, for Control Plane CIoT EPS Optimization, the maximum number of user-data-carrying NAS messages) that the UE is allowed to send within a given time period while attached to that PLMN. Its purpose is to protect the serving PLMN's signalling/control-plane resources from congestion caused by frequent small data transfers or signalling exchanges (e.g., when using CP-CIoT optimization for data transport via ESM DATA TRANSPORT messages), by limiting the rate at which the UE can initiate such control-plane transactions. The UE stores this value and enforces it locally, ensuring it does not exceed the allowed number of uplink NAS transactions per unit time for that serving PLMN.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301 clause 6.6.1a / Annex on ESM information: 'The network may include the Serving PLMN rate control IE... to limit the number of uplink data PDUs (or NAS messages) that the UE is allowed to send via the control plane per deca-minute in order to control the signalling load in the serving PLMN.'

results.question: Under what condition is the UE required to include the Device properties IE in a NAS message according to clause 8.2.33.5?
results.reference: The UE must include the Device properties IE when it is configured for NAS signalling low priority.
results.model_answer: Per 3GPP TS 24.301 clause 8.2.33.5, the UE shall include the Device properties IE in a NAS message (e.g., ATTACH REQUEST or TRACKING AREA UPDATE REQUEST) only if the UE is configured for NAS signalling low priority. If the UE is not configured for low priority operation, the IE is omitted since the default behavior corresponds to 'not configured for NAS signalling low priority'. The IE thus serves to explicitly inform the network that the UE has low-priority signalling characteristics as defined in TS 24.368/22.011.
results.evidence: 8.2.33.5 Device properties: This IE is included by the UE if it is configured for NAS signalling low priority.

results.question: How does the UE determine whether to populate the Device properties IE in its NAS signalling?
results.reference: The UE checks its configuration for NAS signalling low priority; if configured for low priority, it includes the IE.
results.model_answer: The UE decides whether to include the Device properties IE purely on the basis of its own internal configuration for 'NAS signalling low priority', not on any network indication or roaming state. If the UE has been configured (typically by the ME, e.g. via device management/OMA-DM settings for low-priority/MTC-type devices) to operate with NAS signalling low priority, it shall include the Device properties IE in the relevant NAS request messages (ATTACH REQUEST, TRACKING AREA UPDATE REQUEST, EXTENDED SERVICE REQUEST when requesting PDN connectivity, etc.) with the 'NAS signalling low priority indicator' bit set to 'UE configured for NAS signalling low priority'. If the UE is not configured for low priority operation, it either omits the IE or sets the indicator to 'not configured', and this configuration state persists (and is checked again) each time the UE builds a new NAS request message, since the property can change between messages if reconfigured by the ME.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301, subclause 4.3.7.4 / 9.9.2.9 (Device properties IE): 'The UE shall include the Device properties IE in the ATTACH REQUEST and TRACKING AREA UPDATE REQUEST messages if the UE is configured for NAS signalling low priority, and set the NAS signalling low priority indicator accordingly.'

results.question: What configuration of the UE triggers the inclusion of the Device properties IE as specified?
results.reference: The trigger is the UE being configured specifically for NAS signalling low priority.
results.model_answer: The Device properties IE is included by the UE only when the UE is configured for “NAS signalling low priority”. That is, if the UE’s configuration indicates that it is a low‑priority device (e.g., an MTC/IoT device provisioned for NAS signalling low priority), the UE sets the “low priority indicator” in the Device properties IE and includes this IE in the ATTACH REQUEST or TRACKING AREA UPDATE REQUEST message sent to the network. If the UE is not configured for low priority, the Device properties IE is not included.
results.evidence: TS 24.301, clause 5.5.1.2.2 / 5.5.3.2.2: 'If the UE is configured for NAS signalling low priority, the UE shall include the Device properties IE in the ATTACH REQUEST/TRACKING AREA UPDATE REQUEST message and shall set the low priority indicator in the Device properties IE to “MS is configured for NAS signalling low priority”.'

results.question: Explain the relationship between the UE's NAS signalling priority configuration and the presence of the Device properties IE.
results.reference: The presence of the Device properties IE is directly dependent on the UE being configured for NAS signalling low priority; without this configuration, the IE is not required.
results.model_answer: The Device properties IE is the NAS information element that carries the UE's NAS signalling priority configuration to the network. Per TS 24.301, a UE that is configured for 'NAS signalling low priority' (e.g., an MTC/IoT device provisioned for low‑priority operation via USIM or ME configuration) shall include the Device properties IE, with the 'low priority indicator' set to 'MS is configured for NAS signalling low priority', in EMM messages such as ATTACH REQUEST and TRACKING AREA UPDATE REQUEST (and consequently in the associated ESM PDN CONNECTIVITY REQUEST). If the UE is not configured for low priority signalling, it does not need to include the IE (or includes it indicating 'not configured'), since the default behavior assumes normal priority. Thus, the presence/value of the Device properties IE is a direct signalling manifestation of the UE's internal NAS signalling priority configuration, allowing the network (MME) to identify low-priority devices and apply appropriate overload/congestion control, back-off timers, or differentiated treatment (e.g., extended T3346 timers, access restrictions) as defined for NAS signalling low priority UEs.
results.evidence: TS 24.301 clause 4.3.8: 'If the UE is configured for NAS signalling low priority... the UE shall indicate this by including the Device properties IE with the low priority indicator set to "MS is configured for NAS signalling low priority" in the ATTACH REQUEST or TRACKING AREA UPDATE REQUEST message.'

results.question: Why would a UE initiate a Bearer Resource Allocation Request procedure during an active PDN connection?
results.reference: To request the establishment or modification of dedicated bearer resources for specific traffic flows that require different QoS characteristics than provided by the existing default bearer.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.301, Clause 8.3.8, Bearer resource allocation request
results.model_answer: A UE initiates the UE Requested Bearer Resource Allocation procedure (TS 24.301 clause 6.5.2) when it needs the network to allocate additional dedicated EPS bearer resources for a new traffic flow aggregate (TFA) within an already active PDN connection, but does not need to establish a new PDN connection. This is typically triggered by an upper-layer/application request that specifies particular QoS requirements (e.g., guaranteed bit rate, traffic class) for a specific IP flow or set of flows that cannot be adequately served by the existing (default or dedicated) EPS bearer's QoS/TFT. The UE sends a REQUEST BEARER RESOURCE ALLOCATION message containing the linked EPS bearer identity (identifying the PDN connection), the requested traffic flow aggregate description (via Traffic Flow Aggregate description), the requested EPS QoS parameters, and optionally protocol configuration options, asking the network to either establish a new dedicated bearer or modify an existing one to accommodate the new traffic flow with the desired QoS treatment.
results.evidence: TS 24.301 clause 6.5.2.1: 'The purpose of the UE requested bearer resource allocation procedure is to request an allocation of bearer resources for a traffic flow aggregate for the PDN connection using NAS signalling messages, if the UE has already an active PDN connection with the network for the corresponding PDN and no bearer resources with the same...QCI and the same GBR/MBR/APN-AMBR combination have been allocated for the range/type of the given traffic flow aggregate.'

results.question: Why would a UE skip certain requirements upon receiving an ATTACH ACCEPT message during a combined attach for EPS services only when emergency services fallback is pending?
results.reference: The UE skips those requirements because there is a pending request for emergency services and the network indicates it does not support emergency bearer services in S1 mode, forcing the UE to fallback to GERAN or UTRAN to complete the emergency call setup.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.301, Clause 5.5.1.3.4.3, Combined attach successful for EPS services only
results.model_answer: During a combined EPS/IMSI attach, if the network returns EPS services only in the ATTACH ACCEPT while the UE has an emergency services fallback pending, the UE's overriding goal is to quickly complete the EPS attach so it can trigger the fallback (inter-RAT move) to obtain CS emergency service, not to secure combined (CS+PS) service. Since the emergency fallback procedure itself will move the UE out of EPS to place the emergency call, performing the normal 'combined attach was not fully successful' housekeeping (e.g., informing upper layers of a combined-attach failure, retrying combined attach, or invoking the non-EPS-alternative/attach-attempt-counter logic that applies when only EPS services are granted) is unnecessary and could delay or interfere with the pending emergency fallback. Hence the UE is specified to bypass those normal-case requirements and proceed directly with the emergency services fallback procedure.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301 clause 5.5.1.2.4 (Combined attach accepted by the network): 'If the UE requested combined attach and has requested emergency services fallback, and the network returns EPS services only, the UE shall not treat this as a failure of the combined attach procedure and shall not perform the additional requirements applicable when EPS attach result is EPS services only.'

results.question: How does the UE proceed for non-EPS services when it receives an ATTACH ACCEPT message with an EMM cause value not explicitly listed or with no EMM cause IE?
results.reference: The UE considers these as abnormal cases, treats the combined attach procedure as failed for non-EPS services, and follows the behavior specified in clause 5.5.1.3.6 for such failures.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.301, Clause 5.5.1.3.4.3, Combined attach successful for EPS services only
